design_elements.name: 0. Core idea: admission-anchored staging (AAS)
design_elements.rule: Every tier decision for a session's next turn is keyed on one quantity: its predicted admission time Â (when the scheduler will actually start its prefill), not its arrival time as today. One controller covers sessions still in their tool or think gap and sessions already queued. It sets three things: when the SSD fetch starts, what is protected in L2 and for how long, and the eviction order. Sparse load and dense load are handled by the same rule, with no mode switch.
design_elements.signals: Session id, turn-end event, FCFS queue position, EWMA admission rate, L3 read backlog, L2 occupancy (detailed per element below).
design_elements.motivated_by: Paths below are relative to /home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/results/. Arrival-time tiering fails in both measured regimes, by different mechanisms (analysis_gapscale/TAKEAWAYS.md and takeaway_assessment/synthesis.json). Sparse (x70): 19.7% (to) / 18.6% (wc) of returning turns are SSD restores at TTFT p50 2.76 / 3.34 s, against 0.25 / 0.24 s for host hits. Dense (x10/x1): 93-95% of all prefill recomputes context that was in L1+L2 at arrival and on the SSD the whole time. The same x70 load gives hbm_host 61.0 s mean TTFT (crossscale.csv: 60.994) against 1.94 / 1.48 s for the SSD arms, so the cache policy partly creates the regime.

design_elements.name: 1. Session registry
design_elements.rule: At cache_finished_req (turn end t_e), record per live session: a handle to the radix path its last turn committed (last node or page-hash chain, n_s tokens), a per-page residency map (L1/L2/L3), its status (in-gap, queued or running) and Â_s. Update it on arrival and on every scheduling pass.
design_elements.signals: Session id; turn-end event carrying tool-call type and arguments; per-session residency map.
design_elements.motivated_by: The next turn is near-certain and reuses the whole previous context. 4,548 of 4,676 replies (97.3%) are followed by another turn. Storage hits restore about 20.3-20.5K tokens of roughly 29K-token prompts, so fetching a session's last context is wasted only on final turns (about 2.7-3%) (synthesis.json t1). Today nothing persists between turns except LRU stamps: tiers are resolved only at enqueue (prefetch_start lies within 1-2 ms of ReqTimeStats entry_time, n=4,659/4,660).

design_elements.name: 2. Predicting the admission time Â
design_elements.rule: In-gap session: Â = t_e + Ĝ_q + Ŵ. Ĝ_q is a low quantile (q about 0.1-0.25) of the return-time distribution for that tool type, or a harness hint or live progress signal when one exists. Ŵ = (requests ahead) / μ̂, where μ̂ is the EWMA admission rate. Queued at FCFS position p: Â = now + p/μ̂, refined by expected completions of the running batch. While a tool is overdue, re-estimate from the residual gap distribution. On arrival, replace Ĝ with the true arrival time. Only server-side wait counts.
design_elements.signals: Per-tool gap quantiles learned online; optional declared duration or progress stream; FCFS position; EWMA admission rate; completion estimates for the running batch.
design_elements.motivated_by: Arrival time and admission time diverge by minutes under load: x1 server wait p10/p50/p90 = 6.7 / 111 / 255 s (synthesis.json t2). Prediction error is asymmetric (t1). Over-estimating the gap by 25% or more hides only 0.6-1.3%, while under-estimating by 25% with a 2 s margin still nets 85-88% (-50% nets 55-63%), hence a low quantile. Session-history predictors are within ±25% for only 34-50% of L3-hit turns. The running median under-predicts 98.8-99.0% of them (median error -32% / -43%), nets 54-71% and adds 500-700 GiB of SSD reads against 1,571-1,810 GiB actually read. At realistic cadence (campaign 10, compare_20260923_235624/README.md) all 180 SSD restores per arm followed human pauses of 7.7-33 min (median 22 min), so the gap to predict is the human's, not the tool's. The client's 100-connection cap must be removed first: it put 19.9 s of the 131.2 s mean x1 TTFT on the client side.

design_elements.name: 3. Backlog-aware EDF fetch timing
design_elements.rule: Issue the L3->L2 read for a session's pages not in L1/L2 at S_s = Â_s - (n_s^L3 x 98,304 B / BW + Backlog_EDF(Â_s)/BW + m). BW is the measured SSD read bandwidth, Backlog_EDF is the bytes of pending reads with an earlier Â, and m is about 2 s. Serve reads earliest-Â-first (EDF), not FIFO, as low-priority traffic that yields to demand reads, and pace reads plus write-through to stay under BW. Sparse load (Ŵ about 0): the read starts before arrival, with a lead of about 10-20 s at x70. Dense load (Ŵ much larger than H): it starts after arrival, once the request is within p <= μ̂·(read + backlog + m), about 1-2 positions of the head at x1.
design_elements.signals: n_s^L3 from the residency map, L3 read backlog in bytes, measured SSD read and write bandwidth, Â.
design_elements.motivated_by: At x70 the main cost is waiting behind other restores, not one unhidden read (synthesis.json t1). Mean storage-hit TTFT is 5.18 s (to) / 5.57 s (wc). Of that, 3.01 / 4.43 s (58% / 80%) is waiting for the single L3 read thread, against 0.90 / 0.82 s of own IO. Restores arrive in bursts: 10-s offered demand peaks at 4.09 / 3.94 GiB/s, about 2.1x the 1.88 GiB/s SSD, while the read thread is idle 73-77% of the read span. Hits arriving to an empty queue (37-39% of hits) expose only about 0.7 s and carry 5-7% of fetch-window time; hits arriving at depth >= 5 carry 72-81%. Leading by only the own read time hides 16-24%; a 10 s lead hides 81-91% and a 20 s lead about 100% (oracle arrivals, EDF). Mean returning TTFT would fall 1.94 -> 1.17 s (-40%, to) and 1.48 -> 0.50 s (-66%, wc). Today's waste in the to arm: 64 reads (98 GiB) aborted after a mean 7.42 s wait, and those turns recomputed at 10.41 s mean TTFT.

design_elements.name: 4. Park horizon H (cap on how early a fetch starts)
design_elements.rule: A read never starts earlier than Â_s - H. If Â slips beyond H, drop protection and re-arm the fetch if the pages are later evicted.
design_elements.signals: Â, L2 survival or turnover time, parked bytes.
design_elements.motivated_by: Earlier is not better (synthesis.json t1). Fetched pages are inserted unprotected (unified_radix_cache.py:2024). Applying the run's observed L2 survival curve, re-eviction before use is 0.8-1.2% at a 10 s lead, 4.9-7.3% at 20 s, 20-25% at 30 s and 56-64% at 60 s. Fetching at the end of the reply re-evicts 77% (net 13-19% hidden) and parks 37% of L2 on average, peaking at 100-106%. At 10-20 s leads, parked content averages 5-14% of L2 (peak 27%). These are model numbers, not observations.

design_elements.name: 5. Protection until admission, within an L2 budget
design_elements.rule: For every session with Â - now <= H, protect both its arrival-time L1/L2 match and any pages staged for it, from the moment they are matched or land until admission, when the device lock takes over. Use a soft host priority class, not host_lock_ref. Budget: the sum of n_s over protected sessions must be <= β·(L2 - L1 mirror - write-through reserve); when over, shrink H so only the earliest-Â sessions stay protected. This is a CachedAttention-style window measured in seconds rather than jobs. Little's law sizes it at about μ̂·H·n̄.
design_elements.signals: Â per session, L2 occupancy, mirror size, write-through reserve, protected-budget use.
design_elements.motivated_by: This is the dense-regime prize (synthesis.json t2). At x10/x1, 93-95% of all prefill (49.4-54.4M tokens) recomputes context that was in L1+L2 at arrival. The whole previous context was there for 98.4% (x10) / 99.6% (x1) of returns, yet 49.1-49.3% (x10) and 54.7-54.9% (x1) of returning turns were admitted with only the 7,808-token shared prompt cached. Loss grows with wait at x1: 0% under 10 s, 29-35% at 20-30 s, >= 94% beyond 60 s. Nothing protects the match while the request is queued. No lock is taken when the tail is under 256 tokens (1,167 lost turns at x10, 1,309 at x1). After an L3 miss the lock is dropped within p50 1 ms (1,252 / 1,408 lost turns). It is also dropped at insert. Prefetched-then-evicted pages are only 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens, although 80-87% of real L3 reads at x10/x1 were lost (58/68, 57/66, 12/15, 13/15). Sizing: at x1, 0.362/s x 10 s x 20.6K ≈ 75K tokens ≈ 5% of L2. Pinning the whole queue would need about 1.59M tokens, roughly all of L2, which is infeasible. A hard lock is avoided because _execute_kv_backup skips a backup when evict_host cannot free enough space (unified_radix_cache.py:1410-1414); this has not happened so far (0 occurrences).

design_elements.name: 6. Eviction order by predicted admission (latest Â first)
design_elements.rule: Among unprotected host leaves, evict the latest predicted admission first: the queue tail and sessions with long predicted gaps. Use LRU only for content with no session prediction. This replaces the arrival-time LRU refresh. Do-No-Harm: staging for session s may only evict content whose Â is later than Â_s.
design_elements.signals: Â per registry node; whether the node has a session owner; host eviction rate.
design_elements.motivated_by: Today's order is the worst possible one (synthesis.json t2). The arrival-time match refreshes last_access_time along the matched path (unified_tree_core.py:836-839), and LRUStrategy evicts the smallest last_access_time (evict_policy.py:17-18). So host eviction follows FCFS order and evicts the requests just behind the head, which are admitted next; the blocked head itself is re-stamped on each admission attempt. The queued private context (0.91M at minute 18, 1.71-1.80M at minutes 82-98 at x1) exceeds host-only L2 (at most 0.96M). The pressure is self-reinforcing. At x10, 6,667 of 6,723 evict_host events (52.3M of 53.4M tokens) sit next to a d2h_submit from other requests' prefill completions, mostly recomputes. x10/x1 write 54-58M tokens against 5.3M at x70. Steady host eviction runs at 6.6-7.3K tok/s (host-only share turns over in about 131 s).

design_elements.name: 7. Admission fallback: re-match and re-query L3
design_elements.rule: When the FCFS scan reaches s, re-match L1/L2. If the match is shorter than the registry expects, re-query L3 with the semantics of upstream _prefetch_after_device_hit_loss, and skip s under a deadline while the read runs. Choose load or recompute by cost: backlog + read time against prefill time at current throughput. If s arrives before S_s (gap over-predicted), fetch at arrival, so the worst case is today's behaviour. A final turn (2.7% of replies) releases immediately.
design_elements.signals: Registry-expected match length; current L1/L2 match; L3 backlog; current prefill throughput.
design_elements.motivated_by: Admission never asks the SSD again (synthesis.json t2; verified at HEAD 81124a061). check_prefetch_progress returns True when no prefetch is ongoing (scheduler.py:3817-3821). The paced retry is off by default: hicache_storage_prefetch_retry_poll_interval = 0, max 4 attempts, counted in scheduling passes (arg_groups/fields/memory.py:169-183, scheduler.py:3118-3146). Upstream #39283/#40042 is absent (grep count 0). As a result the SSD tier adds nothing under dense load. Shared-prompt-only admissions: x10 hbm_host 53.4% vs 54.4/54.5% for the SSD arms; x1 58.7% vs 59.3/59.5%. Storage hits: 10/9 (x10) and 3/2 (x1); an L3 query hit >= 256 tokens for only 68/4,538 (x10) and 15/4,548 (x1) returns. Just-in-time reload is affordable: about 0.6-0.7 GiB/s at x1, 32-37% of the SSD.

design_elements.name: 8. Feedback-directed tuning
design_elements.rule: Per regime, measure lateness (fetch finished after admission) and pollution (staged or protected bytes evicted or unused). Adapt q, m, H and β from these, as in feedback-directed prefetching (FDP).
design_elements.signals: Per-fetch deadline miss; staged and protected bytes evicted or unused before admission; SSD read amplification.
design_elements.motivated_by: Prediction error is asymmetric (over-estimate >= 25%: about 0-1% of the gain kept; -25%: 85-88%), and history predictors cost 500-700 GiB of extra reads (synthesis.json headroom_estimates). The x70->x10 switch point is unmapped (no runs at x20-x50), so fixed parameters cannot be trusted across regimes. Success targets from evaluation_plan: SSD read amplification <= 1.2x, and no regime worse than B0.

design_elements.name: 9. Optional capacity lever: mirror reclaim (non-inclusive L1/L2), ablated separately
design_elements.rule: Under host pressure, reclaim the L2 mirrors of idle device-resident nodes whose SSD write has been acked. When such a node is later evicted from the device, demote it straight to L3-only, since the SSD already holds every page. If its Â is near, re-copy it to L2 asynchronously instead. This makes L1/L2 non-inclusive without write_back's synchronous D2H.
design_elements.signals: Mirror size, device-lock state per node, SSD write ack per page, Â.
design_elements.motivated_by: Under write-through, about 40% of L2 (636-656K tokens) mirrors L1 in all 9 runs, so unique L1+L2 capacity is 1.63M, not 2.30M (synthesis.json t2; compare_20260922_023714/README.md). The idle, unlocked part of the mirror is 28.7-30.6% of L2 in the x70 SSD arms, but only 5.9-6.7% (x10) and 3.0% (x1). A session-level LRU model predicts x70 SSD/cold returns would fall from 21.0% to 2.7-4.5% (model, not measured), which would shrink element 3's addressable set 4-8x. write_back avoids the mirror but costs a synchronous D2H of 2.63-2.66 µs/token against 0.052-0.058 µs/token for a demote (about 50x); a sync-D2H counterfactual at x10 costs about 186 s against 3.7 s measured.

regimes.regime: Sparse, bursty: x70 gap scale (campaign 7, compare_20260922_023714). 128 live sessions, SWE-bench replay, gaps p50 about 49 s, offered 1.18 turns/s ≈ 85% of capacity, peak queue 73-79.
regimes.what_fails_today: SSD restores are exposed and serialized. Each restore starts at arrival, on a single FIFO read thread, and restores arrive in bursts, so most of storage-hit TTFT is waiting behind other restores while the SSD is idle on average. Inclusive write-through also wastes about 40% of L2. The SSD tier itself works: without it the same load collapses to minute-scale TTFT.

regimes.regime: Dense, oversubscribed: x10 gap scale (campaign 8, compare_20260922_165655). Gaps p50 7.0 s, closed loop of 128 sessions saturates the server, queue holds most sessions.
regimes.what_fails_today: Context matched in L1/L2 at arrival is evicted while the request waits about 100-150 s. It is unprotected, LRU plus the arrival refresh evicts the queue head first, and the eviction pressure is other requests' write-through of recomputed prompts. Admission never re-queries the SSD, so the SSD tier (which holds every page) contributes nothing, and all host-pool arms coincide.

engine_facts: Fork state: live cache class is UnifiedRadixCache (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py), not HiRadixCache. Code references were re-checked at HEAD 81124a061.

Prefetch at enqueue: Scheduler._add_request_to_queue calls self._prefetch_kvcache(req) and then waiting_queue.append(req) (managers/scheduler.py:3148-3155; the call is at line 3154). prefetch_start is logged within 1-2 ms of ReqTimeStats entry_time.

The enqueue 'prefetch' is only L3->L2, only for the suffix L1+L2 missed, and only if that suffix is >= prefetch_threshold = 256 tokens (unified_radix_cache.py:1759-1769). A shorter suffix adds the rid to _storage_prefetch_missed_rids and returns without any host lock. The L2->L1 load happens at admission via init_load_back (managers/schedule_policy.py:1305-1316).

Single L3 read thread, FIFO: prefetch_io_aux_func takes operations one at a time from prefetch_buffer (managers/cache_controller.py:447-448 thread creation, 1136-1141 loop). Measured s2h_io overlaps 4/960 and 0/837.

Admission gating: under wait_complete, admission skips a request until its fetch finishes (check_prefetch_progress, scheduler.py:3817-3821). It returns True when no prefetch is ongoing, so it never re-checks L3. The timeout policy aborts long-waiting reads (x70 to arm: 64 reads, 98 GiB, aborted after 7.42 s).
Prefetch budget is half the host pool, about 814K tokens in flight (cache_controller.py:581). It never bound at x70 (about 60% used).

Fetched pages are unprotected after insert: _handle_prefetch_result inserts and then calls dec_host_lock_ref on the anchor (unified_radix_cache.py:2024; triggered on completed ack at 2562-2566). An L3 hit below threshold revokes the prefetch and releases the lock (2533); the release lands within p50 1 ms of prefetch_start.
The only host lock covering a queued request's arrival match is the prefetch anchor. It is not taken for tails < 256 tokens, dropped after an L3 miss, and dropped at insert.

LRU refresh at match: the matched path's last_access_time is re-stamped at match end (mem_cache/unified_cache/unified_tree_core.py:836-839), and LRUStrategy.get_priority returns last_access_time (mem_cache/evict_policy.py:17-18). Arrival-time matching therefore makes host eviction order follow FCFS arrival order, and the queue head (next to be admitted) goes first. The blocked head is re-stamped on each admission attempt.

Eager write-through: write_through_threshold = 1 under write_through (unified_radix_cache.py:465-467). 72-98% of write volume is triggered when the last prefill chunk completes (cache_unfinished_req with chunked=False, batch_result_processor.py:353-359), before the first token. Intermediate chunks are not backed up separately, and only decode pages plus the boundary page are written at finish.

The SSD write is chained to the host-write ack (h2s lag p50 0.02 s at x70, 0.28-0.34 s at x10/x1). d2h tokens = h2s tokens exactly in all 6 SSD runs, with 0 L3 cleanups, so the SSD holds every context ever written to host. The L3 cleaner (70/60%) was never reached; L3 is effectively unbounded in these runs.

Write-through inclusion: _is_host_leaf (unified_tree_core.py:1889) rejects any node whose device copy still exists (not node.evicted). Under write_through L2 ⊇ L1, and about 40% of L2 (636-656K tokens) mirrors L1 in every run. Unique L1+L2 capacity is 1.63M, not 2.30M.

Only write_back reclaims host duplicates (_reclaim_full_host_duplicates, unified_tree_core.py:1497). It pays a synchronous D2H on device eviction: 2.63-2.66 µs/token against 0.052-0.058 µs/token for a demote (about 50x).

Hard-lock hazard: _execute_kv_backup calls evict_host(needed) and skips the backup (returns None) when it cannot free enough host space (unified_radix_cache.py:1410-1414). Pinning protected content with host_lock_ref could therefore suppress write-through backups (0 occurrences observed so far).

Paced retry exists but is off: hicache_storage_prefetch_retry_poll_interval defaults to 0 and retry_max_attempts to 4 (python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/memory.py:169-183). It counts scheduling passes, not time or admission position (_retry_missed_storage_prefetches, scheduler.py:3118-3146). It is called right after tree_cache.check_hicache_events() in the event loop (scheduler.py:3686-3688), which is also the proposed controller hook.

Upstream SGLang #39283/#40042 (_prefetch_after_device_hit_loss: reactive L3 re-query at admission when the device+host match shrank since arrival, skipping the request meanwhile) is absent from this fork (grep count 0). Upstream HiRadixCache keeps staged L3 pages pinned outside the tree until FCFS-scan finalisation (#32724), so the fork's insert-and-unlock semantics differ.
The campaigns use --schedule-policy fcfs. lpm would order by len(prefix_indices) + host_hit_length (cache-aware admission, untested).

Platform constants: Qwen3-30B-A3B bf16 KV = 98,304 B/token; L1 668,160 tokens (65.7 GB); L2 160 GB = 1,627,648 tokens; SSD /dev/vdc nixl, 1.88 GiB/s read ceiling; recompute P ≈ 4,903 tok/s; shared system prompt 7,808 tokens.
open_questions: Comparison context: CachedAttention (ATC'24, arXiv 2403.19708) as verified from the paper text (takeaway_assessment/citation_verification_journal.jsonl). Disk->DRAM prefetch only for jobs already queued, within a look-ahead window Lpw = Cmem/Skv counted in jobs. An eviction window of (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs: items in it are exempt only from being dropped out of the store entirely, and DRAM->disk eviction takes the window's tail first. Whole-session items. Layer-wise DRAM->HBM pre-loading with a read buffer, and asynchronous saving. No arrival prediction or time signal, so the lead time is bounded by queue wait. No prefix tree or shared prefix, no inclusion or write-through interaction, no SSD-bandwidth or backlog model. Evaluated on ShareGPT with Poisson arrivals: 86% hit rate, 99.6% of hits in DRAM.

Where AAS differs from CachedAttention, per synthesis.json novelty_position: (a) a time horizon from predicted admission instead of a job count, which also covers sessions still in their tool or think gap (pre-arrival fetch); (b) a backlog-aware EDF lead on a contended SSD; (c) protection of the arrival-time L1/L2 match, not only prefetched items, at page granularity with a shared prefix; (d) an eviction key that replaces LRU-refresh-at-match; (e) awareness of write-through inclusion (the mirror-reclaim lever). The synthesis's own framing is "forestall for agentic KV tiers" (Kimbrel et al., OSDI '96), an incremental contribution. It holds only if AAS clearly beats upstream's reactive re-query in the dense regime and keeps most of the oracle gain in the sparse regime with non-oracle prediction.

Gaps relative to CachedAttention that AAS does not address: L3 capacity eviction (CachedAttention's disk-level window, against our unbounded L3 where the cleaner never fired); compute/load overlap such as layer-wise pre-loading or Cake-style compute-while-loading (B9 in the evaluation plan is optional); and the context-overflow truncation that CachedAttention handles.

Threat 1: does a reactive admission-time L3 re-query alone (upstream #39283/#40042 port, or the local paced retry tuned) break the x10/x1 recompute loop? If so, the proactive part saves only about 1 s of read plus backlog per admission against a queue of about 100 s, and the contribution narrows to sparse-regime SSD timing, closest to TokenCake / Ask the Tool. Not yet run (evaluation_plan Step 1).

Threat 2: mirror reclaim alone is predicted (LRU model, not measured) to cut x70 SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5%. That would shrink the sparse-regime addressable set 4-8x. How do the capacity lever and the timing lever combine?

Realism: campaign 10, the only realistic-cadence run, shows neither failure mode. Queue <= 6, SSD <= 34% busy, about 0.6 s of headroom on about 2.6% of turns. The large wins come from x70 (a deterministic 70x stretch) and x10/x1 (oversubscribed closed loops shaped by a 100-connection client cap). What realistic load (more sessions per GPU, smaller L2, bursty human returns, shared L3 across instances) produces the contended or dense regimes?

Predictability: can a human think pause of 7.7-33 min be predicted well enough to stage before arrival? The x70 replay gaps are deterministic, history predictors under-predict exactly the turns that land on L3, and Ask the Tool reports about 80% median error for history predictors. Is a harness hint or live progress signal required? Per-tool quantile predictors are untested.

Closed-loop shift: once recompute stops, admission rate, queue depth and SSD read demand (estimated 32-37% of the SSD at x1) will change. Device KV (668K tokens, about 24 contexts of 28K) may keep x1 queued anyway. Is the dense collapse metastable or purely capacity-driven? The live set exceeds L1+L2 for 42-48% of the x10/x1 runs, so some L3 traffic is unavoidable.
Soft priority class vs hard host_lock_ref for protected content, given the backup-skip path at unified_radix_cache.py:1410-1414.

Write-side inefficiency the design does not yet cover. At x1 about 0.6 GiB/s of SSD writes rewrite recomputed pages whose hashes L3 already holds: does nixl deduplicate? In campaign 10 each SSD arm wrote about 725 GB but read only about 347 GB, with only about 2.6% of turns restored. Could L3 writes be deferred or selected by Â (write only content predicted to outlive L2) to free SSD bandwidth for reads?
Would cache-aware admission (lpm, Strata-style deferral of L2-resident requests) remove the need for protection, and at what fairness or starvation cost?
Transition regime: no runs between x10 and x70 (x20-x50). How does the single rule behave where early and late fetch are both plausible and SSD reads compete with write-through?
Multi-instance: with DP, a shared L3 and a router, session affinity changes which instance's admission time matters.

Upstream semantics differ: HiRadixCache keeps staged pages pinned outside the tree until finalisation (#32724) and has the admission re-query. The diagnosis, especially the literal prefetched-then-evicted case, must be re-checked after a rebase.

Measurement hygiene. All results are single runs, one seed. x10/x1 server queues were shaped by the client's 100-connection cap (fixed afterwards, not re-run). x10 arms 1-3 lack ReqTimeStats. Small inconsistencies to reconcile: x70 to storage restores 890 (compare.csv) vs 896 (TAKEAWAYS); x70 hbm_host mean TTFT 61.0 s (compare.csv) vs 59.5 s (synthesis); campaign 10's unexplained +0.02 s paired p50 cost of the SSD tier.

result.versions_note: Sources read in full (text extracted with PyMuPDF, figures rendered and checked): arXiv 2403.19708 v1 (23 Mar 2024), v2 (16 Apr 2024), v3 (30 Jun 2024); the arXiv HTML v3; and the USENIX ATC '24 camera-ready (atc24-gao-bin-cost.pdf, pp. 111-126). (1) v1 and v2 are titled "AttentionStore: Cost-effective Attention Reuse across Multi-turn Conversations in Large Language Model Serving", and there "AttentionStore" names the whole mechanism. v3 and ATC are retitled "Cost-Efficient Large Language Model Serving for Multi-turn Conversations with CachedAttention": CachedAttention is the mechanism and AttentionStore is only the KV caching system (host memory + disks). (2) A normalized text diff shows v3 and the ATC camera-ready are identical apart from page headers and footers. All quotes below come from v3/ATC. (3) The mechanism text in sections 3.2-3.4 is substantively the same in v1, v2 and v3 apart from the renaming. (4) Evaluation numbers changed between v1 and v2. v1: avg 3.51 turns, about 32K turns, evaluated on 22K; hit rates 76/56/87/89%; TTFT -84/50/88/88%; prefill 6.3/2.0/8.1/8.2x; GPU time 2.7/1.6/2.2/1.7x; cost -56/31/49/35%; at 128G/10T, AS 76% vs LRU 31% and FIFO 48%, with 99.9% of hits in DRAM; overflow ablation hit-rate drops of 52/56/57/48%. v2 and v3 use the numbers given below. (5) v1 and v2 have a "Performance for Long Sequence Inference" section (Mistral-7B, 32K, one A100, a document-analysis session of 6 tasks with 256 input and 64 output tokens each, batch size 1, documents of 4K-28K tokens; TTFT -95%, prefill up to 22x, output throughput +67%). v3 drops that section and adds 4.3.8 "Impact of Session Arrival Rates". v3 still says "We also implement Mistral-7B [19] with a 32K context window" but no longer reports an experiment for it. (6) v3 adds "Continuous batching [57] is enabled through experiments." No version has a limitations or discussion section.

mechanisms.name: AttentionStore: hierarchical KV caching across turns (overall save/reuse model)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Keeps every request's KV cache after its turn ends instead of discarding it. The KV is saved in AttentionStore (host DRAM + SSD). When the session's next turn arrives, the KV is loaded back and only the new turn's tokens are prefilled. HBM is not a cross-turn cache tier here: it holds the execution buffer plus reserved read and write buffers. Keeping KV in HBM only (LMDeploy, RadixAttention) is compared as a baseline.
mechanisms.signals_used: Session identity (KV reused for 'any ensuing conversation turns of the same session'). Reuse is reactive, triggered when the session is 'activated'.
mechanisms.tiers: HBM (execution plus read/write buffers) <-> host memory (DRAM) <-> disks (SSD). Fig. 5: Load/Save between HBM and host memory, Fetch/Evict between host memory and disks.
mechanisms.granularity: Session: one item = all of a session's KV. Storage is managed in blocks (PagedAttention-like allocator). Movement between HBM and host is per layer.
mechanisms.timing_rule: Save when the session goes inactive (in practice asynchronously during the job, see async saving). Fetch and load when the session's next job is queued or executed.
quotes: CachedAttention maintains a hierarchical KV caching system that leverages cost-effective memory/storage mediums to save KV caches for all requests.

Specifically, when the associated conversation session is inactive, CachedAttention saves the KV cache in a KV caching system, named AttentionStore, instead of discarding them as in the conventional attention mechanism. If the same conversation session is activated in the future, its KV cache is fetched from AttentionStore and reused for inference.

Prior works have attempted to reduce the inefficiency of repetitive KV computation by retaining the KV caches across multi-turn conversations in HBMs [18,63]. However, this quickly exhausts the limited HBM capacity.
The host memory and disks are managed in the form of blocks to improve storage utilization, similar to [21]. Our internal storage allocator allocates and deallocates storage blocks on demand.

mechanisms.name: Layer-wise pre-loading (host memory -> HBM) with HBM read buffer
mechanisms.what_it_does: Overlaps loading the historical KV with the prefill of the new tokens, layer by layer. A read stream loads layer i+1 and later layers while the execution stream computes layer i. A reserved HBM read buffer lets loading start while the previous job is still running, which closes the gap between jobs. A larger buffer covers the case where loading takes longer than the partial prefill.
mechanisms.signals_used: The next job to execute, plus per-token load time Tload, per-token prefill time Tpref, historical length Lhist, new-input length Lnew and PCIe bandwidth B (used to size the buffer).
mechanisms.tiers: Host memory -> HBM only. Disk-resident KV must first be fetched to host memory by scheduler-aware fetching. A direct disk-to-HBM path is not described.
mechanisms.granularity: Transformer layer. The buffer size is a byte formula; in the evaluation it is expressed in layers (PL-B0/B5/B10/B15).
mechanisms.timing_rule: Without the buffer, loading starts when the execution buffer frees, i.e. when the last job finishes. With the read buffer it starts 'while the last job is running'. Imperfect overlap occurs when Tload*Lhist > Tpref*Lnew, and the buffer is sized to cover that difference.
quotes: As the GPU executes a layer, the KV cache needed by the subsequent layers can be loaded from the host memory concurrently.
To further mitigate the gap between the last job and the first layer of the current job, CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap.
The read stream can start the pre-loading while the last job is running.
Imperfect overlapping happens when TloadLhist > Tpref Lnew, which indicates that the transmission time is larger than the partial prefilling time.
Combined with the PCIe bandwidth B, the buffer size can be set by the following formula: Sbuf = B(TloadLhist −Tpref Lnew).
For clarity, we use the number of layers to represent the buffer size, e.g., PL-B0 indicates no read buffer and PF-B5 indicates a read buffer size of 5 layers of KV cache.

mechanisms.name: Asynchronous saving (HBM -> host memory) with HBM write buffer
mechanisms.what_it_does: Writes KV back to host memory while compute continues, instead of writing everything after the turn ends. Prefill KV is written layer by layer and overlapped with decoding. Decode KV is written layer by layer as it is produced. Any write still unfinished when decoding ends is moved to a reserved HBM write buffer so the next job is not blocked.
mechanisms.signals_used: Phase (prefill vs decode). No scheduler or session signals.
mechanisms.tiers: HBM -> host memory. Demotion from host to disk is handled separately, by eviction.
mechanisms.timing_rule: Continuous during the job: prefill-phase KV during the decode phase, decode-phase KV per layer while decoding. Leftover writes are drained through the write buffer after the job ends.
quotes: A baseline method to save the KV caches is to write all produced KV caches together after the round of conversation ends. This method however potentially delays the execution of the next scheduled jobs since the KV saving time is on the critical path of inference

for the prefilling phase, as each self-attention operation can produce a significant amount of KV cache, the write stream retains the KV cache layer by layer. The KV cache produced by the prefilling phase can be overlapped with the decoding phase. For the decoding phase, as the KV cache is iteratively produced, the write stream writes back the KV cache layer by layer while decoding.

we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching. The unfinished KV caches are temporarily moved to the write buffer to avoid blocking the execution of the next job.

mechanisms.name: Scheduler-aware fetching (disk -> host memory) with look-ahead prefetching window
mechanisms.what_it_does: Looks at the first Lpw waiting jobs in the scheduler's job queue. A job whose session KV is on disk has that KV prefetched to host memory before the job runs. In Fig. 9, Job 1 is executing and the window covers Jobs 2-3: KV2 is already in DRAM and KV3 is fetched from disk into the DRAM 'buf'.
mechanisms.signals_used: Contents and order of the scheduler's job queue (jobs already arrived), where each waiting job's KV lives (DRAM or disk), Cmem and the average per-session KV size Skv. No timing or prediction signal is used.
mechanisms.granularity: Session: all of a session's KV per job. The window is counted in jobs (queue entries).
mechanisms.timing_rule: Fetch as soon as a queued job enters the head-anchored window of length Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs, where Cmem is 'the available memory capacity for prefetching'. The window is sized by capacity, not by time or bandwidth. Nothing is fetched for a session with no job in the queue.
quotes: Specifically, the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed.

The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv.

As Job 1 is executing, the KV cache manager applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3.

mechanisms.name: Host-memory buffer with threshold-triggered demotion
mechanisms.what_it_does: Reserves free host memory (Fig. 9 marks DRAM regions as 'cache use' and 'sys use'; 'sys use' holds the executing job's KV1 and 'buf') so a disk fetch never waits for space. When free memory falls to a threshold, eviction from host to disk is triggered.
mechanisms.signals_used: Free host-memory capacity against a threshold. The threshold's value is not given.
mechanisms.timing_rule: Eviction is triggered 'When the capacity of the free memory reaches a defined threshold'. The paper gives no number for the threshold or the buffer size.
quotes: Note that CachedAttention includes a host memory buffer that allows for seamless fetching of KV caches from disks to memory, preventing any delays when the host memory is full. When the capacity of the free memory reaches a defined threshold, CachedAttention triggers a KV eviction from host memory to disks to ensure the constant availability of the host memory buffer.

mechanisms.name: Scheduler-aware eviction (host -> disk, disk -> out) with look-ahead eviction window
mechanisms.what_it_does: Uses the queue as future-access information. An item whose job lies in the head-anchored look-ahead eviction window is exempt from eviction out of AttentionStore. For host-to-disk demotion, items nearer the window's tail are evicted first: the scan runs tail to head. In Fig. 9 the window of 6 covers Jobs 2-7 and DRAM holds KV4 and KV2 (cache use). KV4 (Job 4, the latest-queued in DRAM) is demoted. The disk is full, so KV9 is dropped out of the system: Job 9 is queued but outside the window and is 'the last arrived'. KV4 takes KV9's disk slot.
mechanisms.signals_used: Job-queue order (head = next to run, tail = last arrived), whether each cached session has a job in the window, Cmem, Cdisk and Skv. LRU and FIFO are explicitly rejected as history-only.
mechanisms.tiers: Host memory -> disk (demotion). Disk -> out of system (drop).
mechanisms.granularity: Session: 'one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session'. The window is counted in jobs.
mechanisms.timing_rule: Runs when free host memory reaches the threshold or when the disk is full. Window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs, described as a maximum set by total AttentionStore capacity. The order among cached sessions with no queued job is not specified.
quotes: Different from the existing cache eviction strategies, such as the least-recently-used (LRU) [46], first-in-first-out (FIFO) [8], and their variants, which solely rely on the historical access information of the KV caches, CachedAttention presents a scheduler-aware eviction scheme which can leverage the future access information of KV caches to achieve a higher cache hit rate.

The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem +Cdisk)/Skv.

When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted. When CachedAttention evicts one item from the host memory to disks, the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted.

Note that one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session, which is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity in CachedAttention. This is because the KV cache in the same conversation session is either all used or none of it is used.

First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue. It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail. Therefore, the KV cache for Job 4 is selected to be evicted from the host memory to the disks. Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted. Finally, the KV cache for Job 4 is moved to the location previously occupied by Job 9.

mechanisms.name: Positional-encoding-decoupled KV cache truncation
mechanisms.what_it_does: Stores K and V before the relative positional encoding (RoPE) is applied. On context overflow, the stored KV can be truncated directly and the new positions re-applied at load time, so a session's saved KV stays valid instead of being thrown away and recomputed.
mechanisms.signals_used: Context-window overflow (historical tokens exceed the window). The truncation ratio is 0.5 in the evaluation.
mechanisms.tiers: Applies to KV stored in AttentionStore. Positions are re-embedded after loading to HBM.
mechanisms.granularity: Token range within a session's KV.
mechanisms.timing_rule: At load time, when the session's context would overflow the window.
quotes: CachedAttention needs to work with the relative position encoding (RPE) [42, 44, 54].

By simply moving the time of caching KVs before embedding positional encodings in RPE as shown in Figure 11c, CachedAttention can store the KVs without embedded positional encodings in AttentionStore. When reusing the KVs in CachedAttention, the KVs are embedded with the new positional encodings and further used for the following inference.

In the cases where KV cache truncation becomes necessary, the LLM engine retrieves the truncated KV cache (i.e., KV [0:1536]) and loads it to the HBM. The new positional encodings are subsequently applied to the KV cache.

mechanisms.name: Token-discarding-list (TDL) compression compatibility
mechanisms.what_it_does: Lets a KV-compression method (StreamingLLM sink tokens, H2O and similar) name tokens to drop. AttentionStore drops their KV and delivers the pruned KV to the engine. This is described but not evaluated.
mechanisms.signals_used: A TDL produced by an external compression method.
mechanisms.timing_rule: Pruning happens within AttentionStore and the pruned KV is delivered 'upon an inference execution'.
quotes: Specifically, a given KV cache compression technique essentially provides a methodology for creating a token discarding list (TDL), in the prompt, e.g., discarding the least important tokens. CachedAttention straightforwardly complies with the TDL, discarding the KV cache associated with the TDL within the AttentionStore. After discarding the selected KV caches, AttentionStore delivers the pruned KV cache to the inference engine upon an inference execution.

mechanisms.name: Per-session TTL (time to live)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Each session's KV has a maximum retention time measured from its last access. It is introduced only in the capacity-sizing analysis: required capacity CCpUT = DSpUT x CCpS, where DSpUT is distinct sessions per unit time and CCpS is maximum context x per-token KV size. The paper does not say how TTL interacts with the eviction windows.
mechanisms.signals_used: Time since the session's last access.
mechanisms.tiers: All of AttentionStore (stated per session, tier not specified).
mechanisms.timing_rule: Expiry at TTL after last access. TTL = the 'unit time' of DSpUT; 1 hour in the §4.3.6 experiment.
quotes: In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access. The TTL is set as the unit time mentioned above.
In the experiment, we set the TTL to one hour.

By configuring the cache capacity of CachedAttention as CCpUT, we can achieve a cache hit rate of 100% if not considering the newly arrived conversations. Nevertheless, to achieve a high cache hit rate in real scenarios, we do not need to configure such a large capacity since the hotness of cached items is different.

mechanisms.name: Data-movement implementation (CUDA streams and IO threads)
mechanisms.what_it_does: Dedicated CUDA streams move data between GPU and host, overlapping with compute (called 'proactive swapping'). Separate IO threads migrate data between host and disk. The system is built in PyTorch/Python on HF Transformers model code, with continuous batching enabled.
mechanisms.tiers: GPU<->host over CUDA streams; host<->disk over IO threads.
quotes: Dedicated CUDA streams are used for moving data between the GPUs and the host memory, overlapping the computation with proactive swapping. Separate IO threads migrate data between the host memory and the disks, overlapping the execution with the KV cache migrations. Continuous batching [57] is enabled through experiments.

result.sessions_not_in_queue: Not addressed. Nothing is prefetched for a conversation whose next turn has not arrived, and nothing in the paper predicts when a turn will arrive. The only signals are the jobs already in the queue. The fetching rule applies only to 'waiting jobs' in the queue: 'the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed.' Eviction protection also applies only to items whose job is inside the look-ahead eviction window: 'if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted.' Even a session that is queued but outside the window is unprotected: in Fig. 9, Job 9 is queued beyond the size-6 window and its KV is dropped out of the system as 'the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue'. The paper treats returning turns as unpredictable: 'As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks'. Resumption is reactive: 'If the same conversation session is activated in the future, its KV cache is fetched from AttentionStore'. The worked example avoids the no-queued-job case: 'First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue.' So the order among cached sessions with no queued job (LRU, FIFO, size, or anything else) is never stated. The paper rejects LRU and FIFO as the primary policy but gives no fallback. The only rule that applies to an idle session is the TTL in §4.3.6: 'the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access', set to one hour there. That is an expiry rule, not a priority. The paper never models inter-turn think time (the words 'think', 'interval' and 'next turn' do not appear). Fetches therefore start only when a turn enters the queue, so their lead time is bounded by queueing delay. This last point is my inference from the text, not a claim the paper makes.
result.eviction_policy_details: Item = one whole session's KV, and fetching uses the same granularity: 'the minimal eviction and fetching granularity'. Trigger for demotion from host to disk: free host memory reaches 'a defined threshold'. The value is not given; the aim is to keep a host-memory buffer available for fetches. Trigger for dropping from disk: 'if the disks are full'. Look-ahead eviction window: head-anchored over the job queue, with length (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs, described as the 'maximum length' and 'determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore'. Exemption rule: an item whose job is in the window is never evicted out of AttentionStore. Demotion order: 'the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted'. The scan runs 'from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail', so the session whose queued job will run last is demoted first, which approximates Belady's rule using queue position. Drop order (from Fig. 9): the 'last arrived' queued job outside the window (Job 9) is dropped first, and the demoted item 'is moved to the location previously occupied by Job 9'. Unspecified: the order among items with no queued job, any LRU or recency tiebreak, and how TTL expiry interacts with the window. Symbol ambiguity: Cmem is 'available memory capacity for prefetching' in §3.3.1 but appears in a 'total storage capacity' formula in §3.3.2. The paper argues for this policy against LRU and FIFO: 'which solely rely on the historical access information of the KV caches'. Its ablation (Fig. 21) compares CA against LRU and FIFO baselines that also lack prefetching ('LRU and FIFO lack awareness of future KV cache information and cannot pre-fetch KV caches from disks to host memory'). So the contributions of fetching and of eviction are never measured separately; this is my observation. Sizing check (my arithmetic, not from the paper): with 0.78 MB/token for LLaMA-13B and about 2K-token sessions, 10 TB of disk gives an eviction window of thousands of jobs, which likely covers the whole queue in practice.
result.write_path_details: HBM to host memory: asynchronous and layer-wise during the job, not after it. Prefill KV is 'retain[ed] layer by layer' and its write is overlapped with the decoding phase. Decode KV is written back 'layer by layer while decoding'. A reserved HBM write buffer takes 'unfinished KV caches' so the next job is not blocked. The rejected baseline was to 'write all produced KV caches together after the round of conversation ends'. Dedicated CUDA streams carry the GPU<->host traffic. KV is saved 'for all requests' (abstract). Host memory to disk: not write-through. KV reaches disk by demotion, which is eviction triggered by the free-memory threshold, running on 'Separate IO threads' that 'migrate data between the host memory and the disks, overlapping the execution with the KV cache migrations'. 'most KV caches are retained in disks' as a result of that eviction. Inclusive or exclusive tiers: never stated explicitly. The wording is migration-style ('evict ... from the host memory to disks', 'migrated to the host memory', 'the KV cache for Job 4 is moved to the location previously occupied by Job 9'), which suggests exclusive placement. Fig. 9 shows KV3 still drawn on disk while it is being fetched into the DRAM 'buf', so whether the disk copy is kept after a fetch is not addressed. Storage is block-managed ('managed in the form of blocks ... similar to [21]'). Measured effect: asynchronous saving cut total execution time by 13-15% (LLaMA-13B, 1 GPU, batch 16, prompts of 1K-1.6K tokens, 20 decode steps).
result.queue_and_admission_model: The scheduler is taken as given and is not modified. CachedAttention only reads its queue: 'the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs'. The queue has a 'head', where the next job runs and both windows are anchored, and a tail holding the 'last arrived' job. This implies execution in arrival (FIFO/FCFS) order, although the terms FCFS and first-come never appear. Admission order is known simply by reading the queue position of jobs that have already arrived. Nothing reorders jobs by cache location (for example running DRAM-resident sessions first), and preemption, priorities, SLOs and multi-instance routing are not discussed. Window lengths are in jobs and are derived from capacity, Cmem/Skv and (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv, using an average per-session KV size Skv. They take no account of time or of disk bandwidth or backlog. The paper assumes queued jobs give enough lead time for a disk-to-DRAM fetch, but never states the lead time or the queue depth. Execution uses continuous batching ('Continuous batching [57] is enabled through experiments'); in v3 the paper notes that with continuous batching 'each newly arrived job must complete prefilling before it can join other decoding jobs'. The paper does not say what happens when a job reaches the head while its KV is still on disk or mid-fetch (stall, recompute, or load straight from disk). It also does not say whether TTFT includes queueing delay; TTFT is defined only as 'how quickly users start seeing the output of LLMs after entering their prompt'.
result.truncation_and_context_overflow: Problem: when history exceeds the context window, engines drop the oldest tokens. That invalidates saved KV because the positions baked into it (RoPE on K) change. The paper's evidence: '47% and 30% of conversation sessions have a context longer than 2K and 4K'. Solution: cache K and V before the positional encoding is applied and re-apply new positions at load time ('By simply moving the time of caching KVs before embedding positional encodings in RPE ... When reusing the KVs ... the KVs are embedded with the new positional encodings'). This requires relative positional encoding ('CachedAttention needs to work with the relative position encoding (RPE)'), e.g. LLaMA, Falcon, Mistral; absolute-PE models are excluded. Example in Fig. 10: a 4K window with a 2K truncation. Example in Fig. 12: pos[0:2048] becomes pos[0:1536] and the engine 'retrieves the truncated KV cache (i.e., KV [0:1536]) and loads it to the HBM'. In the evaluation, 'the token truncation ratio is set to 0.5, implying that when an overflow occurs, the system will discard the earliest half of the tokens'. The TDL hook allows compression-based selective retention. Accuracy: PPL is within 0.02 of recompute-based token truncation (TT) on WikiText-2, PTB and C4 for LLaMA-7B/13B (e.g. WikiText-2 LLaMA-7B CA 5.47, TT 5.48, naive KV truncation NKVT 2198.7). On MMLU, LongEval and PIQA, CA is close to TT (e.g. MMLU LLaMA-13B 52.3% vs 53.2%) while NKVT collapses (29.6%). Performance: compared with OF, which keeps positions embedded so overflow invalidates the cache, CA's hit rates are higher by 17.6/41.5/18.1/18.4 points for LLaMA-13B/65B/70B/Falcon-40B. LLaMA-65B suffers most because of its 2K window. The cost of re-applying RoPE at load is not quantified.

evaluation.models_hardware: Testbed: 'All our experiments are performed on 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each with 80GB HBM. The system is equipped with 128GB DRAM and 10TB SSDs. GPUs are connected to the host via PCIe Gen 4.' Implemented in PyTorch/Python with HF Transformers model code and continuous batching. Models: LLaMA-1 65B; LLaMA-2 13B and 70B; Falcon-40B; FP16. 'LLaMA-13B operates on two GPUs with 24 batches, while LLaMA-65B, LLaMA-70B, and Falcon-40B run on four GPUs, handling 24 batches each.' Per-token KV: LLaMA-65B 2.5 MB, LLaMA-13B 0.78 MB, LLaMA-70B 0.31 MB, Falcon-40B 0.12 MB (GQA). Mistral-7B with a 32K window is mentioned in v3, but its experiment appears only in v1/v2. Micro-benchmarks use LLaMA-13B on 1 A100 with batch 16. Accuracy tests use LLaMA-7B/13B. Motivating figures from §2.4: about 26 GB/s effective PCIe Gen4 x16, so loading 2K tokens (5 GB) of LLaMA-65B KV takes about 192 ms against about 360 ms to prefill them; disks run at under 5 GB/s.
evaluation.workloads: ShareGPT (90K raw conversations; 73% multi-turn; 30% exceed 4K tokens). End-to-end runs use 9K sessions with an average of 5.75 turns, about 52K turns in total: 'We warm up AttentionStore using the first 10K conversation turns and then evaluate the performance on the following 42K turns.' Micro-benchmarks use synthetic history/new splits (500/500 up to 900/100 tokens; 1K history + 100 new; prompts of 1K-1.6K with 20 decode steps). Accuracy uses WikiText-2, PTB, C4, MMLU, LongEval and PIQA, with a long text inserted to force truncation.
evaluation.arrival_and_think_time: Session arrivals only: 'As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0).' §4.3.8 sweeps 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s; the figure axis runs to 2.5. Think time between turns of a session is not addressed: the paper never says how or when a session's later turns arrive (immediately after the previous answer, after a delay, or interleaved). Queue depth and lead time before execution are not reported.
evaluation.tier_capacities: Default 128 GB DRAM and 10 TB SSD. The eviction ablation uses 128G/2T, 128G/5T and 128G/10T. The storage-medium comparison uses an HBM-only cache of 10 GB, HBM+DRAM (128 GB), and CA (128 GB DRAM + 10 TB SSD). The capacity study sweeps storage capacity / CCpUT from 0 to 0.35 with TTL = 1 h. The overflow ablation uses 128 GB/10 TB. The arrival-rate study uses LLaMA-13B with 128 GB/10 TB. The split of host memory between prefetch slots, buffer and cache, and the threshold value, are not given.
evaluation.baselines: End-to-end: RE (recomputation), which keeps only token history, discards KV after each turn, and truncates on overflow at ratio 0.5. Placement ablation: CA vs LRU and FIFO eviction, which also lack prefetching. Overflow ablation: OF, with positions embedded, so overflow invalidates the cache and forces recompute. Accuracy: TT (token truncation + recompute) and NKVT (naive KV truncation with positions left embedded). Caching-medium ablation: HBM-only (10 GB) and HBM+DRAM. There is no head-to-head comparison with another KV-offload system (Pensieve, LMDeploy and RadixAttention appear only in related work).
key_results: Total KV hit rate (DRAM + disk): 86% / 71% / 89% / 90% for LLaMA-13B / 65B / 70B / Falcon-40B. LLaMA-65B is lower because of its 2.5 MB/token KV.
TTFT reduced by 85% / 61% / 87% / 86% vs RE (headline 'up to 87%').

End-to-end GPU time speedup 4.0x / 1.9x / 3.3x / 3.4x vs RE. The paper credits less prefill recompute, no recompute after overflow, and decode no longer blocked by long prefills under continuous batching.
Cost (AWS on-demand: $5/h per A100, $0.0088/h/GB DRAM, $0.000082/h/GB SSD): 70% / 43% / 66% / 68% savings vs RE. Storage is 16.4% / 9.0% / 9.0% / 9.0% of CA's cost.
Layer-wise pre-loading (LLaMA-13B, 1K history + 100 new tokens): with no read buffer (PL-B0), prefill time is -35% vs no pre-loading. A 15-layer buffer (PL-B15) overlaps the load fully: -61%.
Asynchronous saving reduces total execution time by 13-15% (prompts of 1K-1.6K, 20 decode steps).

Scheduler-aware fetch + evict vs LRU/FIFO: at 128G/2T the overall hit rate is +27% vs LRU and +31% vs FIFO. At 128G/10T: CA 86% vs LRU 58% vs FIFO 48%; GPU time up to 2.7x better. DRAM hits are about 0.5% for LRU and FIFO (128G/2T: 0.5% DRAM + 12.4% disk for LRU, 0.5% + 9.0% for FIFO) versus over 99.6% of CA's hits being DRAM hits.
Decoupled truncation: compared with OF, CA's hit rates are higher by 17.6 / 41.5 / 18.1 / 18.4 points, with matching GPU-time gains. PPL is within 0.02 of TT; NKVT PPL is above 10^3.
Capacity: at RCC/CCpUT = 0.1 the hit rate is 51%; at 0.25 it is 98% (TTL 1 h).
Storage mediums: HBM-only (10 GB) hit rate is about 0%. HBM+DRAM reaches 3.4 / 1.7 / 7.7 / 19.1%. CA (with SSD) reaches 86 / 71 / 89 / 90%.

Session arrival rate from 0.5 to 2.0/s (LLaMA-13B): hit rate falls from 82% to 77%, TTFT rises from 0.122 s to 0.154 s, prefill throughput falls from '858K/s to 681K/s' (the figure axis is in k/s), and GPU time rises from 6.25 H to 7.01 H. The paper calls the impact 'minimal'.

limitations_stated: The paper has no limitations, threats or discussion section. The items below are caveats stated in the text, followed by gaps I identified.
Requires relative positional encoding: 'CachedAttention needs to work with the relative position encoding (RPE)'. Models with absolute positional encoding cannot use decoupled truncation.
Pre-loading can fall short: 'Imperfect overlapping happens when TloadLhist > Tpref Lnew'. This needs a larger HBM read buffer, Sbuf = B(TloadLhist − Tpref Lnew), which costs HBM.

Disk is slow and turn arrivals are treated as random: 'the disks have an access bandwidth of less than 5 GB/s. As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks when being accessed'. The paper's mitigation depends on jobs already being queued.

Per-token KV size limits the hit rate: 'Given the same available storage space, CA accommodates fewer sessions for LLaMA-65B, thereby limiting the hit rate' (71%). A 2K context window makes overflow frequent: 'OF of LLaMA-65B experiences a low hit rate due to its limited 2K context window.'
First turns cannot hit: capacity sizing gives 100% hits only 'if not considering the newly arrived conversations'.
Hit rate falls with load: from 82% to 77% as session arrival rate rises from 0.5 to 2.0/s, 'a lower DSpUT results in higher hit rates'.
Storage is not free: it is 16.4% of total cost for LLaMA-13B and 9% for the other models.
Synthetic timing: 'As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution'.

Not addressed (gap): any prediction of when a session's next turn arrives, prefetch or protection for sessions with no queued job, eviction order among unqueued sessions, inter-turn think time, the host-buffer threshold value, behaviour when a job reaches the head with its KV still on disk, disk-read backlog and bandwidth contention in window sizing, multi-node or cluster routing, cross-session prefix sharing, whether TTFT includes queueing, and an ablation separating fetching from eviction.

challenges.claimed_difference: Core idea: AAS keys every tier decision on one predicted admission time Â in seconds, where CachedAttention (CA) uses windows counted in jobs.
challenges.counterargument: For a session that is already queued, AAS sets Â = now + p/μ̂ under FCFS with a single EWMA rate. That is a strictly increasing function of queue position p. Every ordering decision (who to fetch next, who to protect, who to demote) is therefore identical to CA's head-anchored window ordering. Seconds only change the window's length, and AAS converts that straight back to capacity: when protected bytes exceed β·(L2 − mirror − reserve), it 'shrinks H so only the earliest-Â sessions stay protected'. That is CA's Lpw = Cmem/Skv expressed in bytes instead of an average Skv. Using each session's own n_s instead of the mean Skv is an implementation refinement, not a design idea. Refining Â with running-batch completion estimates changes magnitudes, not order. The obvious extension of CA to agents is to insert a placeholder job at each in-gap session's predicted position and let CA's windows do the rest. So 'one quantity' re-parameterizes CA for queued work, and its real content reduces to the in-gap case (challenge 2) and bandwidth timing (challenge 3).
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: An experiment where time and job count really diverge: context sizes from about 5K to 100K tokens, admission with variable service times, or a mix of in-gap and queued sessions. In it, a faithful CA baseline (B4: Lpw = Cmem/Skv prefetch, tail-first demotion, window exemption) given the same byte budget must lose measurably to AAS. Without B4 in the evaluation, no 'beyond CachedAttention' claim can be made at all.

challenges.claimed_difference: Pre-arrival SSD staging: AAS starts the L3->L2 read for sessions still in their tool or think gap, while CA fetches only for jobs already in the queue.
challenges.counterargument: This is true against CA as published: CA never predicts arrivals, and its fetch lead is bounded by queue wait. It does not hold against CA's natural extensions or the agentic literature. Prediction-timed restore is published for DRAM->HBM: TokenCake (predictive upload as the predicted function-call completion approaches, EuroSys '27), Ask the Tool (refresh one lead time before the predicted return), SYMPHONY (advisories carrying expected_arrival), and KVFlow, PBKV and SAGA (prefetch the next agent's KV). For storage it is announced by NVIDIA Dynamo (prefetch hooks), vLLM AgentX and llm-d. Moving the source tier from DRAM to SSD changes a constant. The evidence is also oracle-only: 'a 10 s lead hides 81-91%' uses the replay's true arrivals. The one realistic predictor tested (session history) nets only 54-71% and adds 500-700 GiB of SSD reads, and per-tool quantiles are untested. In the realistic-cadence run (campaign 10), all 180 SSD restores per arm followed human pauses of 7.7-33 min, which tool-type quantiles cannot predict, and the available win is about 0.6 s on about 2.6% of turns. x70 is a deterministic 70x stretch of trace gaps, the one setting where prediction is trivially easy.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: (1) A non-oracle predictor (per-tool quantile, harness hint or progress signal) that keeps at least about 70% of the oracle gain at x70 with resampled stochastic gaps. (2) A head-to-head against B6 (TokenCake/Ask-the-Tool style: lead equals own transfer time, no backlog or queue term, no protection) showing the SSD tier needs AAS's extra terms. (3) A realistic workload (more sessions per GPU, smaller L2, L3 shared across instances, bursty human returns) where SSD restores are frequent and contended enough to matter.

challenges.claimed_difference: Backlog-aware EDF fetch timing on a contended SSD: lead = own read time + bytes of earlier-deadline reads / BW + margin. Reads are served earliest-Â-first and yield to demand reads.
challenges.counterargument: Against CA this is a real difference, since CA's windows have no time, bandwidth or backlog term. As an idea it is Kimbrel et al.'s forestall (OSDI '96): prefetch earlier when misses bunch up (i·F >= d_i), just in time otherwise. EDF for deadline I/O is textbook real-time disk scheduling, and 'speculative reads must be bounded and yield to demand' is py-kvcache's lesson. Inside CA's frame, a long queue already gives a deep lead, because a fetch fires as soon as a job enters Lpw. Backlog therefore matters only when the queue is short, which is the pre-arrival case again. The team's own numbers suggest the backlog term may be unnecessary. A fixed 20 s lead hides about 100% at x70, with 4.9-7.3% re-eviction and parked content at 5-14% of L2, and a fixed 10 s lead hides 81-91%. A fixed, generous lead (TokenCake plus a margin) may capture nearly all of the gain without modelling backlog. Part of the backlog is also caused by this fork: a single FIFO read thread (s2h overlap 4/960) and write-through traffic that CA does not have, since CA writes to disk only on demotion.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: An ablation at equal SSD read amplification and equal parked bytes comparing: lead = own read time (FIFO), fixed 10 s and 20 s leads, and backlog-aware EDF. It must show backlog-aware EDF is Pareto-better on TTFT against parked bytes and re-eviction. The strongest cases are the burst peaks (4.09 GiB/s offered against 1.88 GiB/s) and a 0.5x throttled-SSD run. The win must also hold after the read path allows several outstanding reads, so it is not an artefact of the single thread.

challenges.claimed_difference: Protecting the arrival-time L1/L2 match, not only prefetched pages, until admission, within an L2 budget.
challenges.counterargument: CA's scheduler-aware eviction already covers every cached item whose job is in the window, however the item got there. Those items are exempt from being dropped, and DRAM->disk demotion scans tail to head, so the next sessions to run stay in DRAM. In this system L3 holds every page (write-through, and the cleaner never fired), so evicting from L2 is exactly CA's 'demote to disk'. 'Protect the head within an L2 budget' is therefore CA's tail-first demotion. The dense-regime evidence shows this fork lacks CA's mechanism, not that CA falls short: 93-95% of prefill recomputes context that was in L1+L2 at arrival, because LRU plus refresh-at-match evicts the queue head first. CA rejects LRU and FIFO explicitly and reports an 86% hit rate against 58% and 48% for them. Neighbouring prior art covers the rest. Continuum keeps GPU KV pinned while the program's next request is in the waiting queue. KVFlow sets per-radix-node priority by steps to execution. PCR bumps waiting requests' chunks in its look-ahead LRU. vLLM #50014 pins unread promotions, and upstream SGLang #39283 adds a full pin under staged fetches. Soft priority versus a hard lock is an engine detail forced by unified_radix_cache.py:1410-1414.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Run B4 and the Step-1c 'queue-position eviction only' ablation at x10/x1. If either matches AAS, drop the claim. It survives only if something CA lacks matters measurably. Candidates: protecting device-resident (L1) KV across turns, which CA cannot do because its HBM is not a cross-turn tier; shared-prefix or partial-match pages; or AAS's just-in-time fetch window freeing L2 for protection so that recompute falls clearly below what CA's capacity-sized prefetch window achieves.

challenges.claimed_difference: Eviction ordered by latest predicted admission, replacing the LRU refresh at match, plus a Do-No-Harm guard on staging.
challenges.counterargument: CA's demotion rule is that 'the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted'. That is Belady's rule approximated by queue position, and CA adopted it explicitly in place of LRU and FIFO. For queued sessions, AAS's 'latest Â first' is the same rule. Ordering in-gap content by predicted next use is KVFlow (steps to execution per radix node), PBKV (K-step look-ahead reuse score) and SAGA (WA-LRU with per-tool TTL). Do-No-Harm is Rule 3 of Cao, Felten, Karlin and Li (SIGMETRICS '95). Removing this fork's refresh-at-match behaviour is a bug fix, not a contribution.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: The only part left is ranking in-gap and queued sessions on one axis (challenge 6). Show cases where that axis decides differently and wins. Example: an in-gap session with Ĝ of about 5 s should outrank a queued session at position 50 with Ŵ of about 100 s, whereas CA exempts the queued one and leaves the in-gap one in an unspecified order. Count how often this happens in the traces and what it does to TTFT.

challenges.claimed_difference: One controller across the sparse and dense regimes with no mode switch: Â = t_e + Ĝ_q + Ŵ combines the gap and the queue wait.
challenges.counterargument: A single rule that is aggressive when I/O-bound and late when compute-bound is the defining property of forestall. Combining a tool-duration distribution with a queueing-delay estimate is Continuum's formula: P(τ,f)·(T·η + reload), with T a sliding-window queue delay. Continuum uses it for GPU retention rather than fetch timing, but the combination exists. In the regimes actually measured, one term dominates. At x10/x1, Ŵ of about 100-150 s dwarfs Ĝ, so AAS behaves like CA's queue window. At x70, Ŵ is about 0, so AAS behaves like TokenCake or Ask the Tool with an SSD lead. 'AAS = CA plus TokenCake' therefore stands until shown otherwise in the intermediate regime, and that regime was never run (no x20-x50 runs). The dense-regime benefit is not measured either: the synthesis says 'x10/x1 TTFT cannot be estimated from these runs'. Queue wait there was shaped by the client's 100-connection cap, and every result is a single seed.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Runs at x20-x50 (plus a throttled SSD and varied L2) where one AAS parameter set beats the best of B3 (reactive re-query), B4 (CA) and B6 (TokenCake-style) in every regime, including the transition where Ĝ and Ŵ are comparable. Add Ĝ-only and Ŵ-only ablations of Â.

challenges.claimed_difference: Admission fallback: re-match L1/L2, re-query L3 when the match has shrunk, and choose load or recompute by cost.
challenges.counterargument: This is already merged upstream: SGLang #39283 adds _prefetch_after_device_hit_loss and #40042 keeps its retry budget available. KVFlow's status-aware scheduling already skips requests whose nodes are still loading. Choosing load or recompute by cost appears in TokenCake's T_fc vs T_transfer gate, Continuum's Prefill-Reload term and Cake-style compute-while-loading. CA leaves the case of a job reaching the head with its KV on disk unspecified, but filling that gap is engineering. Worse, this element is Threat 1. If the reactive re-query alone removes most dense-regime recompute, the proactive part saves about 1 s of read against a queue of about 100 s, and the dense-regime claim collapses.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Nothing makes this element novel. Present it as a safety net. To keep the dense-regime claim, AAS must clearly beat a ported B3 on recompute share, TTFT and admissions/s, per the plan's own criterion: recompute below 10% and better than B3.

challenges.claimed_difference: Park horizon H: a cap on how early a fetch may start, because early staging gets re-evicted.
challenges.counterargument: This is TIP's prefetch horizon (Patterson et al., SOSP '95) and the fixed-horizon component of forestall, and CA's windows are bounded too. The motivating numbers (20-25% re-eviction at a 30 s lead, 56-64% at 60 s) are modelled from survival curves, not observed. They also depend on this fork inserting fetched pages and then unlocking them (unified_radix_cache.py:2024), while upstream HiRadixCache keeps staged pages pinned outside the tree (#32724). Once protection (element 5) exists, H is a budget parameter, not a mechanism.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Measured, not modelled, re-eviction against lead time after rebasing onto upstream staged-page semantics, showing that H still changes outcomes.

challenges.claimed_difference: Awareness of write-through inclusion: mirror reclaim, making L1/L2 non-inclusive, with direct L3-only demotion.
challenges.counterargument: CA never has this problem. Its HBM holds only the executing job plus read/write buffers, not a cross-turn cache, and its DRAM->disk movement is described as migration, which suggests exclusive tiers. Making a hierarchy exclusive is old (Wong and Wilkes, DEMOTE, USENIX ATC '02), and SGLang's own write_back mode already reclaims host duplicates. The lever is independent of Â. By the team's own LRU model it would cut x70 SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5%, shrinking AAS's sparse-regime addressable set 4-8x. It moves the design toward CA and undercuts the significance of the timing lever.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Show that the Â-guided variant (re-copy to L2 only when Â is near, demote straight to L3 otherwise) beats plain mirror reclaim and write_back. Report capacity alone, timing alone and both together, so it is clear what the timing lever adds once capacity is fixed.

challenges.claimed_difference: Page-level, prefix-tree granularity with a shared prefix, against CA's whole-session items, plus a per-session registry of residency and status.
challenges.counterargument: This is the substrate, not the design. RadixAttention/HiCache, PCR's prefix tree of 256-token chunks, and KVFlow's per-node priorities already work at this granularity. CA argues that session granularity is right for multi-turn chat because the session's KV is 'either all used or none of it is used'. The shared 7,808-token system prompt is a constant that any policy keeps hot. The registry is bookkeeping that CA performs implicitly through its per-session items and per-session TTL.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Show that partial residency matters: fetching only the n_s^L3 suffix instead of whole-session items saves measurable SSD bandwidth in the contended regime. Alternatively, show that shared-prefix pages create protection conflicts a session-level CA cannot express.

challenges.claimed_difference: Per-tool low-quantile gap prediction (q about 0.1-0.25), justified by the asymmetric cost of errors, with feedback-directed tuning of q, m, H and β.
challenges.counterargument: Per-tool percentile fits for TTLs are in SAGA, per-function EWMA prediction in TokenCake, and per-tool empirical CDFs in Continuum. Feedback-directed prefetching is Srinath et al. (HPCA '07). 'A late prefetch only loses its benefit while an early one pollutes the cache' is classic prefetching theory. Feedback-directed tuning is neither implemented nor evaluated. The gaps that actually reach the SSD at realistic cadence are human pauses, not tool calls, so tool-type quantiles do not address them, and Ask the Tool reports that history-based predictors are poor.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Show that the quantile predictor, or a harness hint, works on the turns that end up on the SSD. Show that feedback-directed tuning finds suitable parameters online across the x70 to x1 sweep, including the unmapped transition regime.

challenges.claimed_difference: The measurements show arrival-time tiering fails in both regimes, so a new design beyond CA is needed.
challenges.counterargument: The failures were measured on a fork that lacks CA's mechanisms and has defects of its own: the LRU refresh at match evicts the queue head; tails under 256 tokens get no lock; pages are unlocked at insert; there is one FIFO read thread; admission never re-queries L3; and the paced retry is off by default. The diagnosis therefore argues for 'implement CA and the upstream fixes', not for AAS. The only realistic-cadence run (campaign 10) shows neither failure mode: peak queue 3-6, SSD at most 34% busy, and only -0.14 s mean against hbm_host. x70 is a deterministic 70x stretch. x10/x1 are oversubscribed closed loops shaped by a 100-connection client cap. Every result is a single run, and no B4 run exists, so 'beyond CachedAttention' has no evidence yet.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Implement B4 faithfully in the same engine. Re-run x70, x10 and x1 with the client cap removed and at least 3 seeds. Find a realistic configuration (more sessions per GPU, 80 GB L2, L3 shared across DP instances, bursty human returns) where B4 still fails and AAS does not.

challenges.claimed_difference: AAS subsumes CachedAttention: CA is the special case where Ĝ is infinite for unqueued sessions.
challenges.counterargument: Subsuming CA is not novelty, and AAS is not a superset. It lacks CA's layer-wise DRAM->HBM pre-loading with a read buffer (35-61% less prefill time), its asynchronous layer-wise saving with a write buffer (13-15% less execution time), any disk-capacity eviction (AAS assumes an unbounded L3; the cleaner never fired), and position-decoupled truncation. CA also writes to disk only on demotion, whereas AAS's substrate writes every page: about 725 GB written against 347 GB read per SSD arm in campaign 10, and about 0.6 GiB/s at x1, mostly rewriting recomputed pages. That write traffic uses the SSD bandwidth AAS then has to schedule around.
challenges.what_would_rescue_it: Add elements CA cannot express. (1) Â-gated SSD write admission: write or defer L3 copies only for content predicted to outlive L2, freeing bandwidth for reads. (2) Â-keyed L3 capacity eviction: drop the latest-Â content first, i.e. CA's disk window measured in time. (3) Layer-wise L2->L1 overlap for host hits. The first two would be differences CA's job-queue signal cannot produce.

ca_claims: CachedAttention appeared at USENIX ATC '24 (arXiv 2403.19708). v1 and v2 were titled 'AttentionStore'. In v3/ATC, AttentionStore names only the KV caching system (host DRAM + SSD).
CA saves KV caches for all requests in a host DRAM + SSD hierarchy (AttentionStore) instead of discarding them. It fetches them back when the same session is activated again.

In CA, HBM is not a cross-turn cache tier. It holds the execution buffer plus reserved read and write buffers, and HBM-only retention (LMDeploy, RadixAttention) is treated as prior work or a baseline.
CA's disk->DRAM prefetch applies only to waiting jobs in the scheduler's job queue. They must lie within a head-anchored look-ahead prefetching window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs.
CA's windows are counted in jobs and sized by capacity, using the average per-session KV size Skv. They contain no time, disk-bandwidth or read-backlog term.
CA's look-ahead eviction window is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs long. An item whose job is inside it is exempt from eviction out of AttentionStore.
For DRAM->disk demotion, CA evicts the item nearest the tail of the look-ahead eviction window first, scanning from tail to head.
In CA's Fig. 9 example, the KV of a queued job outside the window (Job 9, 'the last arrived') is dropped out of the system.
CA explicitly rejects LRU and FIFO because they 'solely rely on the historical access information of the KV caches'.
CA's minimal eviction and fetching unit is one whole session's KV, justified because a session's KV 'is either all used or none of it is used'.
CA makes no prediction of when a session's next turn will arrive. Nothing is fetched or protected for a session with no queued job, and the eviction order among such sessions is not specified.
