CA's only rule for idle sessions is a TTL measured from last access (1 hour in §4.3.6). It appears only in the capacity-sizing analysis, and its interaction with the eviction windows is not specified.
CA does not model inter-turn think time. Its evaluation uses ShareGPT with Poisson session arrivals (λ = 1.0, swept from 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s).
CA states that because conversation requests arrive randomly, their KV caches are more likely to be on disk when accessed.
My inference, not stated in the paper: because CA fetches only for queued jobs, its disk-fetch lead time is bounded by each job's queueing delay.
CA does not modify the scheduler. It reads the job queue, whose head and tail imply FCFS execution, and it does not reorder jobs by cache location.
CA does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk or mid-fetch.
CA saves KV asynchronously and layer by layer during the job. An HBM write buffer holds unfinished writes, and this cut total execution time by 13-15%.

CA overlaps layer-wise DRAM->HBM pre-loading with prefill, using an HBM read buffer sized Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew). Prefill time fell 35% with no buffer (PL-B0) and 61% with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15).
In CA, KV reaches disk only through demotion triggered when free DRAM reaches a threshold, not by write-through. The threshold value is not given.
CA describes tier placement in migration-style language, which suggests exclusive tiers, but never states whether the tiers are inclusive or exclusive.
CA stores K and V before the positional encoding is applied, so saved KV can be truncated on context overflow. This requires relative positional encoding.
CA has no prefix tree and no cross-session prefix sharing.

CA's eviction ablation compares it with LRU and FIFO baselines that also lack prefetching, so the contributions of fetching and eviction are never measured separately. At 128G/10T the hit rates are CA 86%, LRU 58% and FIFO 48%.
In that ablation, over 99.6% of CA's hits are DRAM hits.
CA's total KV hit rates are 86/71/89/90% for LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-65B, LLaMA-70B and Falcon-40B.
CA's hit rate falls from 82% to 77% as the session arrival rate rises from 0.5 to 2.0/s (LLaMA-13B).

CA was evaluated on 4 A100-80GB GPUs with 128 GB DRAM and 10 TB SSD over PCIe Gen4. It was implemented in PyTorch on HF Transformers model code with continuous batching, using dedicated CUDA streams for GPU<->host transfers and separate IO threads for host<->disk.
CA notes that disks have under 5 GB/s of access bandwidth.
CA has no head-to-head comparison with another KV-offload system, and the paper has no limitations or discussion section.
surviving_differences: Pre-arrival staging from the SSD for sessions with no queued job, timed from a predicted return. CA as published has nothing for these sessions; its lead time is bounded by queue wait (my inference). The difference holds against CA, but not against the agentic DRAM->HBM line (TokenCake, Ask the Tool, SYMPHONY, KVFlow, PBKV, SAGA) except in two respects: the source tier is the SSD and Â includes a queue-wait term. The evidence so far is oracle-only.

When a fetch starts depends on bandwidth and backlog, and SSD reads are ordered EDF. CA's windows have no time, bandwidth or backlog term, and TokenCake, Ask the Tool and SYMPHONY have no contention term. This is defensible as forestall applied to a contended KV storage tier, but it still needs an ablation against a fixed 10-20 s lead at equal read amplification and parked bytes.

One time axis ranks in-gap and queued sessions together for fetching, protection and eviction. CA cannot rank sessions with no queued job, since their order is unspecified. Continuum combines a tool-duration CDF with queue delay, but only for GPU retention TTLs, not fetch timing or multi-tier eviction. The difference is narrow and only matters in the unmeasured x20-x50 transition regime, where Ĝ and Ŵ are comparable.

The empirical characterization on SWE-agent traces in a three-tier radix engine. (1) 58-80% of storage-hit TTFT is spent waiting behind bursty restores while the SSD is about 75% idle. (2) Arrival-time matches are invalidated during queueing, because LRU refresh-at-match evicts the queue head. (3) Inclusive write-through wastes about 40% of L2. (4) The cache policy shifts the operating point: 61 s mean TTFT without the SSD tier against 1.5-1.9 s with it at x70. This holds as a measurement contribution, with the caveats that the failures are partly fork-specific, every result is a single seed, and none of them appears at realistic cadence.

Problems that arise only in an engine where HBM is a cross-turn cache tier and the SSD is written through, both of which CA avoids by design. They are: protecting KV without suppressing write-through backups (soft priority instead of host_lock_ref, because of the backup-skip path), protecting device-resident KV across turns, and Â-guided non-inclusive demotion. These count as engineering for HiCache-style engines, not as a core novelty.
The robustness analysis of asymmetric prediction error, with a fallback that is never worse than today's arrival-time behaviour. It holds as analysis, but is not yet validated end to end.

Candidates that would differ from CA if built, because CA's job-queue signal cannot express them: Â-gated SSD write admission or deferral (CA writes to disk only on demotion, and AAS's substrate writes every page), and Â-keyed L3 capacity eviction (CA's disk window measured in time rather than jobs).

dimensions.dimension: What is predicted, and when the fetch is triggered
dimensions.cachedattention: Nothing is predicted. The trigger is the real job queue. When a waiting job enters a head-anchored look-ahead prefetching window, its disk-resident KV is fetched into host memory before the job runs. Queue position stands in for admission order. The fetch can only start after the job has arrived.
dimensions.ours: AAS predicts Â, the time the scheduler will start the session's prefill, for every live session. For a session in its gap, Â = t_e + Ĝ_q + Ŵ; for a queued one, Â = now + p/μ̂. The L3->L2 read starts at Â − (own read + EDF backlog + m), but no earlier than Â − H.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Today's fork already fetches at enqueue. That matches CachedAttention's fetch trigger whenever the window covers the queue: the prefetch budget is ~814K tokens, about 40 restores of ~20.3K tokens, and it never filled at x70 (~60% used). So the x70 SSD arms roughly measure CachedAttention-style fetching, though not its eviction order. Under it, 890 (to) / 837 (wc) returning turns (19.6% / 18.6%) were SSD restores, with mean TTFT 5.18 / 5.57 s; 58% / 80% of that was waiting behind other reads. With oracle arrivals and EDF, a lead before arrival hides 81-91% of fetch time at 10 s. A 20 s lead cuts mean returning TTFT 1.94 -> 1.17 s (-40%) and 1.48 -> 0.50 s (-66%). These are simulations with oracle arrivals, not measurements of AAS.

dimensions.dimension: Sessions still in their idle gap (no queued job)
dimensions.cachedattention: Not addressed. Nothing is fetched or protected until a turn is queued. The order among cached sessions with no queued job is not specified. The only rule that touches idle sessions is a 1-hour TTL in the capacity analysis. The paper treats returning turns as arriving randomly.
dimensions.ours: In-gap sessions are first-class. Each gets an Â from a low quantile of the per-tool or human-pause return-time distribution, or from a harness hint, plus the predicted server wait. They can be staged before arrival, protected once Â − now ≤ H, and ranked for eviction by Â.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Time-averaged requests in flight (queued plus running), computed from turns_three_tier_to.csv as summed latency over the run: 10.9 of 128 sessions at x70 and 14.3 of 80 in campaign 10. So about 89% / 82% of sessions are in their gap at any moment, where a queue-only policy has no information. Every x70 L3-hit gap was ≥ 46.9 s (to) / 47.9 s (wc), so lead time exists. 37-39% of storage hits arrived to an empty queue. The SSD was idle 73-77% of the read span, yet 10-s demand peaked at 4.09 / 3.94 GiB/s against 1.88 GiB/s; only reads issued before arrival can move that burst into idle time. In campaign 10 all 180 restores per arm followed human pauses of 7.7-33 min (median 22 min). Hiding their 0.62 s fetch saves ~0.6 s on ~2.6% of turns, about 0.016 s on the mean (my arithmetic). Whether those pauses can be predicted is not shown: history predictors under-predict 98.8-99.0% of L3-hit turns.

dimensions.dimension: Units of look-ahead: jobs vs seconds
dimensions.cachedattention: Jobs. The prefetching window is Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs and the eviction window is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs. Both are sized by capacity and average per-session KV size, with no term for time, disk bandwidth or read backlog.
dimensions.ours: Seconds. The lead is own read time + EDF backlog + margin m. It is capped by the park horizon H. Protection is budgeted as β·(L2 − mirror − write-through reserve), and Little's law sizes it at ≈ μ̂·H·n̄.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: The same number of jobs means very different lead times. At x1, μ̂ ≈ 0.362 admissions/s, so the needed lead is only 1-2 queue positions. At x70, the needed 10-20 s lead usually covers jobs that have not arrived yet. Parking cost grows with time, not with jobs. From the observed L2 survival curve, unprotected staged pages are re-evicted at 0.8-1.2% for a 10 s lead, 4.9-7.3% at 20 s, 20-25% at 30 s and 56-64% at 60 s, and 77% when fetching at the end of the reply (model). A capacity-sized window at x1, e.g. the fork's ~40-session prefetch budget, means ≈ 110 s of lead at 0.362/s (my arithmetic). That is close to the ~131-145 s L2 turnover. A 10 s horizon at x1 is ≈ 75K tokens ≈ 5% of L2.

dimensions.cachedattention: Contents and order of the job queue; where each waiting job's KV lives (DRAM or disk); Cmem, Cdisk and Skv; a free-host-memory threshold; session identity for reuse. No timing or prediction signal. LRU and FIFO are rejected because they rely only on historical access information.
dimensions.ours: Session id. Turn-end event with tool-call type and arguments. Per-tool gap quantiles and human-pause statistics, or an optional harness hint or progress signal. FCFS position. EWMA admission rate. Expected completions of the running batch. L3 read backlog in bytes. Measured SSD read and write bandwidth. L2 occupancy and mirror size. Per-page L1/L2/L3 residency.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: L3 backlog is the signal that matters at x70. A lead of only the own read time hides 16-24%; a 10 s lead that covers the backlog hides 81-91%. A simulation of one FIFO reader reproduces the observed io_end (median error -0.029 s), and while requests waited for the read thread it was busy with other reads 99.5-99.7% of the time. The admission-rate signal matters under load: at x1, server wait p10/p50/p90 was 6.7 / 111 / 255 s, so arrival time is a poor proxy for admission. The tool-type signal is weak at realistic cadence: restores follow human pauses, not tool calls. Per-tool quantile predictors are untested. History predictors net 54-71% of the oracle gain.

dimensions.dimension: Tier hierarchy and the disk->host path
dimensions.cachedattention: HBM holds the execution buffer and reserved read/write buffers and is not a cross-turn cache. AttentionStore is host DRAM plus SSD. Disk->DRAM movement is scheduler-aware fetching. DRAM->disk movement is threshold-triggered eviction (demotion).
dimensions.ours: Same three media, but L1 GPU memory is a cross-turn radix cache (inherited from SGLang). AAS changes only the timing and order of L3->L2 reads and L2 residency. L2->L1 still happens at admission (init_load_back).
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: The data supports CachedAttention's core thesis that a disk tier is needed. At the same x70 load, mean returning TTFT is 61.0 s for hbm_host and 97.0 s for hbm_lru (GPU-only), against 1.94 / 1.48 s with the SSD. Keeping L1 as a cache helps only a little beyond host: in campaign 10, device-hit turns average 0.328 s TTFT and host-hit turns 0.411 s. AAS's difference lies in timing, covered in other rows, not in the hierarchy.

dimensions.dimension: Host->GPU transfer: layer-wise overlap and read buffer
dimensions.cachedattention: Layer-wise pre-loading. A read stream loads layers i+1 onward while layer i computes. A reserved HBM read buffer lets loading start while the previous job runs, sized as Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew). Without the buffer (PL-B0) prefill time drops 35%; with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15) it drops 61%.
dimensions.ours: Not part of AAS. The fork inherits SGLang HiCache's layer-wise H2D load at admission: LayerDoneCounter (cache_controller.py:71-96) with a per-layer wait in the KV pool (memory_pool.py:1425-1426). There is no read buffer that stages before admission.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: The host->GPU path costs little here. Campaign 10, three_tier_to: host-tier turns average 0.411 s TTFT (p50 0.314 s) against 0.328 s (p50 0.277 s) for device-tier turns, on ~27K-token prompts. At x70, host p50 is 0.248 s against device 0.297 s. A CachedAttention-style read buffer at L2->L1 could save at most ~0.04-0.08 s per host hit.

dimensions.dimension: Granularity: session item vs radix-tree pages with a shared prefix
dimensions.cachedattention: One item is all of a session's KV. This is the minimal unit for eviction and fetching, justified because a session's KV is either all used or none. Storage is block-managed. Cross-session prefix sharing is not addressed.
dimensions.ours: Radix-tree pages with per-page L1/L2/L3 residency. The 7,808-token shared system prompt is stored once. The session registry adds a session-level handle (the last committed radix path) for prediction, but stages only the pages missing from L1/L2 (n_s^L3).
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: SSD restores read about 70% of the prompt. At x70 that is 20.3K of 29.1K tokens (to) and 20.5K of 28.9K (wc); in campaign 10 it is 19.1K of 27.8K. The rest, mostly the shared prompt, stayed resident. A whole-session item would read ~1.4x the bytes on an SSD already 2.1x oversubscribed at 10-s peaks. Storing the shared prompt per session would take 128 × 7,808 ≈ 1.0M tokens, ≈ 61% of the 1,627,648-token L2 (my arithmetic). CachedAttention's all-or-none premise does hold for private context: 97.3% of replies are followed by a turn that reuses the whole previous context. That is why AAS keeps prediction at session level.

dimensions.cachedattention: An item whose job is inside the look-ahead eviction window is exempt from being dropped out of AttentionStore. DRAM residency is governed only by demotion order; nothing is pinned in DRAM. A queued job outside the window is unprotected (Job 9 in Fig. 9 is dropped).
dimensions.ours: A soft host priority class, not host_lock_ref. It protects both the arrival-time L1/L2 match and any staged pages of sessions with Â − now ≤ H, until admission. The total is capped at β·(L2 − mirror − reserve), and H shrinks when the cap is exceeded.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Our L3 never dropped anything: 0 L3 cleanups, and d2h = h2s in all 6 SSD runs. So CachedAttention's drop exemption would do nothing here; the loss happens in L2. At x10/x1, 93-95% of prefill recomputes context that was in L1+L2 at arrival. 49.1-49.3% (x10) and 54.7-54.9% (x1) of returning turns lost the whole private context. At x1, loss by wait is 0% under 10 s, 29-35% at 20-30 s and ≥ 94% beyond 60 s. Pinning the whole queue would need ≈ 1.59M tokens, all of L2, which is infeasible. A 10 s horizon needs ≈ 75K tokens (5% of L2). Caveat: the fork has neither CachedAttention's tail-first order nor a re-fetch for queued jobs, so this loss shows the fork is worse than CachedAttention, not that AAS beats it.

dimensions.cachedattention: Host->disk demotion takes the item nearest the tail of the look-ahead eviction window first (scan from tail to head), which approximates Belady using queue position. When the disk is full, the last-arrived queued job outside the window is dropped. The order among sessions with no queued job is not specified.
dimensions.ours: Among unprotected host leaves, evict the latest Â first: the queue tail and sessions with long predicted gaps. LRU applies only to content with no session owner. Do-No-Harm: staging for s may only evict content with a later Â. This replaces the LRU refresh at arrival-time match.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Today the arrival-time match re-stamps last_access_time (unified_tree_core.py:836-839), and LRU evicts the smallest stamp (evict_policy.py:17-18). Host eviction therefore follows FCFS arrival order and evicts the requests just behind the queue head first, the opposite of CachedAttention's rule. At x10, 6,667 of 6,723 evict_host events (52.3M of 53.4M tokens) sit next to other requests' d2h writes. With ~89% of x70 sessions in their gap, CachedAttention's rule says nothing about most cached sessions in the sparse regime. Ordering versus capacity is unresolved: a session-level LRU model predicts that mirror reclaim alone would cut x70 SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5% (model).

dimensions.dimension: Disk-tier capacity: drop policy and TTL
dimensions.cachedattention: A disk drop happens when the disk is full and exempts items in the eviction window. Each session has a TTL (1 hour in the experiment) from last access, used in capacity sizing (CCpUT). At capacity ratio 0.1 the hit rate is 51%; at 0.25 it is 98%.
dimensions.ours: None. L3 was effectively unbounded: the 70%/60% cleaner was never reached.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: 0 L3 cleanups in all runs. Each campaign 10 SSD arm wrote 7.37M tokens ≈ 725 GB in a 2-hour window, about 8.7 TB/day (my arithmetic). Any long-running deployment needs an L3 drop policy, and an Â-ordered drop with a TTL is the natural analogue of CachedAttention's disk window.

dimensions.cachedattention: Layer-wise asynchronous saving. Prefill KV is written layer by layer, overlapped with decoding; decode KV is written per layer while decoding. An HBM write buffer takes unfinished writes so the next job is not blocked. This cuts execution time by 13-15%.
dimensions.ours: Inherited from the fork: write-through D2H is triggered when the last prefill chunk completes (72-98% of write volume), before the first token. The SSD write is chained after the host-write ack. Decode pages and the boundary page are written at finish. AAS only adds pacing of writes against reads.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Both keep saving off the critical path. h2s lag p50 is 0.02 s at x70 and 0.28-0.34 s at x10/x1. We have not measured write interference on TTFT. Campaign 10's unexplained +0.02 s paired p50 cost of the SSD tier is one candidate (unverified).

dimensions.cachedattention: HBM is not a cross-turn cache, so HBM and DRAM never hold duplicates. KV reaches disk by demotion, not write-through. Inclusive vs exclusive placement is never stated. The wording ('moved', 'migrate') suggests exclusive, and whether the disk copy is kept after a fetch is not addressed.
dimensions.ours: In the fork, write-through makes L2 ⊇ L1 and L3 ⊇ L2. AAS identifies the cost and offers an optional lever: reclaim L2 mirrors of idle device nodes whose SSD write is acked, then demote them straight to L3-only (non-inclusive L1/L2). It also raises Â-selected L3 writes as an open question.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: About 40% of L2 (636-656K tokens) mirrors L1 in all 9 runs, so unique L1+L2 is 1.63M tokens, not 2.30M. The idle mirror is 28.7-30.6% of L2 at x70 but only 3.0-6.7% at x10/x1. Amplification: campaign 10 wrote 7.37M tokens (~725 GB) and read 3.53M (~347 GB) while restoring only 2.6% of turns. x1 wrote 57.97M tokens, mostly rewrites of recomputed pages already on SSD. Demote-on-evict, as in CachedAttention, would barely reduce writes here (events_three_tier_to.csv). Host evictions were 56.6M tokens at x1 against 58.0M written through, and 9.3M in campaign 10 against 7.37M. At x70 evictions were 21.8M against 5.27M written, because 18.1M tokens had been re-read from SSD; if disk copies were not kept, demotion would write ~4x more. The bigger lever is that the write path never checks whether L3 already holds a page: write_backup_storage (unified_radix_cache.py:1632) -> _page_backup (cache_controller.py:1266) -> nixl batch_set_v1 (hicache_nixl.py:847). This matches d2h = h2s exactly. Lower nixl layers were not checked. Precedent for the remedy: exclusive caching / DEMOTE (Wong & Wilkes, ATC '02).

dimensions.dimension: I/O scheduling: read order, FIFO vs EDF, bandwidth contention
dimensions.cachedattention: GPU<->host transfers use dedicated CUDA streams; host<->disk transfers use separate IO threads. The order in which disk reads are served is not specified. Window sizing ignores disk bandwidth and backlog.
dimensions.ours: Reads are served earliest-Â-first (EDF) as low-priority traffic that yields to demand reads. The lead includes the EDF backlog. Reads plus write-through are paced to stay under the measured bandwidth.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: The fork has one FIFO read thread (cache_controller.py:1136-1141). s2h IO overlapped only 4/960 (to) and 0/837 (wc) times. The read-thread wait was 3.01 / 4.43 s of the 5.18 / 5.57 s mean storage-hit TTFT, while the thread was idle 73-77% of the read span. Caveat: when every read is issued at arrival and admission is FCFS, FIFO order already equals EDF order. EDF only pays off once reads are issued before arrival, out of admission order. The EDF-vs-FIFO ablation has not been run. On contention: at x1, write-through (~0.6 GiB/s) plus just-in-time reloads (0.6-0.7 GiB/s) would use ~65-70% of 1.88 GiB/s, assuming reads and writes share one budget (my arithmetic).

dimensions.dimension: Misprediction handling and fallback at admission
dimensions.cachedattention: Nothing to mispredict: it acts only on queued jobs, whose order is known. The paper does not say what happens when a job reaches the queue head with its KV still on disk or mid-fetch.
dimensions.ours: Use a low quantile of the gap (q ≈ 0.1-0.25). Re-estimate from the residual gap when a tool is overdue. If the session arrives before S_s, fetch at arrival. At admission, re-match L1/L2 and, if the match shrank, re-query L3 (upstream _prefetch_after_device_hit_loss semantics); skip the request under a deadline and choose load vs recompute by cost. Tune q, m, H and β from lateness and pollution (FDP).
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: The error cost is asymmetric (x70 simulation). Over-estimating the gap by ≥ 25% keeps only 0-1% of the gain, i.e. falls back to today. Under-estimating by 25% with a 2 s margin nets 85-88%; by 50%, 55-63%. Session-history predictors are within ±25% for only 34-50% of L3-hit turns. They net 54-71% and add 500-700 GiB of reads on top of 1,571-1,810 GiB (about +28-45%), against a target of ≤ 1.2x. The fallback is needed: the fork never re-queries the SSD at admission (check_prefetch_progress returns True when no prefetch is in flight, scheduler.py:3817-3821). An L3 query found ≥ 256 tokens for only 68/4,538 (x10) and 15/4,548 (x1) returns. In the x70 to arm, 64 reads (98 GiB) were aborted after a mean 7.42 s wait, and those turns recomputed at 10.41 s mean TTFT.

dimensions.cachedattention: Two queue mechanisms aim squarely at this case. Demotion is tail-first, so sessions near the head stay in DRAM. Disk-resident KV of jobs inside the prefetching window is fetched before they run.
dimensions.ours: Protect the match in seconds within a budget, evict by latest Â, re-query L3 just in time (~1-2 positions before the head at x1), and decide load vs recompute by cost.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: At x1 the queued private context (0.91M growing to 1.71-1.80M tokens) exceeds host-only L2 (≤ 0.96M). Any policy, CachedAttention's included, must reload part of the queue from SSD; just-in-time reload needs ≈ 0.69 GiB/s (32-37% of the SSD). AAS differs here in three ways: page-level protection of the arrival-time match, a budget in seconds, and the admission re-query. No CachedAttention-faithful baseline or upstream #39283 baseline has been run, so the gain over CachedAttention in this regime is unknown.

dimensions.cachedattention: Stores K and V before RoPE and re-applies positions at load, so saved KV can be truncated on overflow (ratio 0.5) instead of discarded. Requires relative positional encoding. PPL is within 0.02 of token-truncation recompute. Hit rates are 17.6 / 41.5 / 18.1 / 18.4 points higher than the OF baseline. A token-discarding-list hook is described but not evaluated.
dimensions.ours: Not handled. AAS has no overflow, truncation or compaction mechanism.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Never exercised: the largest prompt was 57,600 tokens (x70/x10/x1) and 90,612 (campaign 10), against a 131,072-token window, so no turn overflowed. Agent harnesses that compact context by rewriting it would invalidate the prefix in both designs. That case is untested.

dimensions.cachedattention: Assumes a queue exists. Because fetches start only when a job is queued, their lead time is bounded by that job's queueing delay (my inference, not stated in the paper). Evaluated at 0.5-2.0 sessions/s; the hit rate fell from 82% to 77% across that range. Queue depth and lead time are not reported.
dimensions.ours: One rule with no mode switch. With an empty queue the read starts before arrival (a 10-20 s lead at x70). Under a long queue it starts 1-2 positions before the head (x1).
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Each regime fails differently. At x70, storage-hit TTFT is dominated by the read backlog. At x10/x1, recompute is 54-59% of tokens and SSD hits are 0.22% / 0.07% of tokens, with mean TTFT 115-131 s for every host-pool arm. Campaign 10 shows neither failure (peak queue 3-6, SSD ≤ 34% busy). Gaps: no runs between x10 and x70, and the x10/x1 queues were shaped by a 100-connection client cap. All runs are single-seed, and AAS itself has not run in any regime.

dimensions.dimension: Evaluation workload realism (think time, agentic tool gaps)
dimensions.cachedattention: ShareGPT: 9K sessions, 5.75 turns on average (~52K turns), warm-up on the first 10K turns and evaluation on the next 42K. Session arrivals are Poisson (λ = 1.0, swept 0.5-2.0/s). Inter-turn think time is not modeled. Testbed: 4× A100 80GB, 128 GB DRAM, 10 TB SSD.
dimensions.ours: SWE-bench agent replays with long prompts (p50 ~23.6K tokens) and gaps scaled x70/x10/x1. Campaign 10 adds a cadence calibrated to TraceLab: tool p50 0.1 s / p90 10 s, and a human pause after 1 in 8 calls (p50 1.4 min, p90 20.6 min, capped at 30 min). Platform: H200 with Qwen3-30B-A3B.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Realism cuts both ways. At realistic cadence, returning TTFT is already 0.35-0.36 s for the SSD arms (0.45 s for hbm_host). Only ~2.6% of turns are SSD restores, each with ~0.6 s to hide. The large AAS headroom comes only from x70 (a deterministic 70x stretch) and x10/x1 (closed loops shaped by the client cap). All results are single runs.

dimensions.cachedattention: Implemented in PyTorch with HF Transformers model code and continuous batching, and measured end to end. Hit rate 86/71/89/90%; TTFT -85/61/87/86% vs recomputation; cost -70/43/66/68%. At 128G/10T, 86% hit rate vs 58% for LRU and 48% for FIFO, with over 99.6% of hits served from DRAM. Fetching and eviction are ablated only together.
dimensions.ours: AAS is not implemented. Its benefits are oracle or model estimates. The two main threats are unresolved: upstream #39283's reactive re-query alone, and mirror reclaim alone.
dimensions.evidence_from_our_data: Every headroom figure (-40% / -66% at x70; recompute dropping from 93-95% of prefill at x10/x1) comes from simulations with oracle arrivals or survival-curve models. Measurements so far describe only today's fork.

ca_claims: CachedAttention (USENIX ATC '24; arXiv 2403.19708 v3) saves the KV caches of all requests in AttentionStore, a KV caching system made of host DRAM and SSDs, and reuses them for later turns of the same session.
In CachedAttention, HBM holds the execution buffer plus reserved read and write buffers and is not used as a cross-turn KV cache tier.
CachedAttention does not predict when a session's next turn will arrive or be admitted.
CachedAttention's scheduler-aware fetching prefetches disk-resident KV into host memory for waiting jobs inside a head-anchored look-ahead prefetching window over the scheduler's job queue.
The prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs, where Cmem is the host memory available for prefetching and Skv is the average per-session KV size.
The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs, described as a maximum set by the total capacity of AttentionStore.
Both windows are counted in jobs, sized by capacity, and take no account of time, disk bandwidth or read backlog.
Nothing is prefetched for a session that has no job in the queue.
An item whose job is inside the look-ahead eviction window is exempt from being evicted out of AttentionStore.
For host-to-disk demotion, the item at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has the highest priority to be evicted (the scan runs tail to head).
In the paper's Fig. 9 example, when the disk is full, the KV of the last-arrived queued job outside the size-6 window (Job 9) is dropped out of the system.
The paper does not specify the eviction order among cached sessions that have no queued job.
The paper rejects LRU and FIFO because they rely solely on historical access information.
CachedAttention gives each session's KV a TTL measured from its last access; it appears only in the capacity-sizing analysis and is set to one hour in that experiment.
In the capacity study (TTL 1 h), the hit rate is 51% at a capacity ratio (RCC/CCpUT) of 0.1 and 98% at 0.25.
In CachedAttention, one item is all of a session's KV; this is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity, justified because a session's KV is either all used or none of it.
AttentionStore manages host memory and disks in blocks.
The paper does not address cross-session prefix sharing.
Layer-wise pre-loading overlaps loading the KV of later layers from host memory with the computation of the current layer.
An HBM read buffer lets pre-loading start while the previous job is still running.
The read-buffer size is set by Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew).
With LLaMA-13B, 1K history plus 100 new tokens, pre-loading cuts prefill time by 35% with no read buffer (PL-B0) and by 61% with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15).
Asynchronous saving writes prefill-phase KV layer by layer, overlapped with decoding, writes decode-phase KV layer by layer while decoding, and moves unfinished writes to an HBM write buffer.
Asynchronous saving reduces total execution time by 13-15%.
In CachedAttention, KV reaches disk by demotion (eviction triggered when free host memory reaches a threshold), not by write-through.
The paper does not give the value of the host-memory threshold.
The paper never states whether its tiers are inclusive or exclusive; its migration wording ('moved', 'migrate') suggests exclusive placement.
The paper does not say whether the disk copy is kept after a KV cache is fetched into host memory.
CachedAttention uses dedicated CUDA streams for GPU-host transfers and separate IO threads for host-disk migration.
The paper does not specify the order in which disk reads are served.
The paper does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk or being fetched.
Because CachedAttention fetches only for jobs already in the queue, a fetch's lead time is bounded by the job's queueing delay (an inference from the fetch rule, not stated in the paper).
The paper treats conversation requests as arriving randomly.
CachedAttention takes the scheduler as given and only reads its job queue; execution from the queue head in arrival order is implied, though FCFS is never named.
CachedAttention stores K and V before the positional encoding is applied and re-applies new positions at load time, so saved KV can be truncated on context overflow.
Positional-encoding-decoupled truncation requires relative positional encoding.
In the evaluation, the truncation ratio is 0.5 (the earliest half of the tokens is discarded on overflow).
Perplexity with CachedAttention's truncation is within 0.02 of recompute-based token truncation.

Compared with the OF baseline (positions embedded, so overflow invalidates the cache), CachedAttention's hit rates are higher by 17.6 / 41.5 / 18.1 / 18.4 points for LLaMA-13B / 65B / 70B / Falcon-40B.
CachedAttention describes compatibility with token-discarding lists (TDL) from KV-compression methods but does not evaluate it.
The evaluation uses ShareGPT with 9K sessions averaging 5.75 turns (about 52K turns): the first 10K turns warm up AttentionStore and the following 42K are evaluated.
Session arrivals are generated from a Poisson distribution with λ = 1.0 sessions/s, and §4.3.8 sweeps 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s.
The paper does not model inter-turn think time.
The paper does not report queue depth or the lead time before execution.
The testbed is 4 NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs, 128 GB DRAM and 10 TB SSDs, connected over PCIe Gen4.
CachedAttention is implemented in PyTorch with HF Transformers model code, and continuous batching is enabled in the experiments.
Total KV hit rates are 86% / 71% / 89% / 90% for LLaMA-13B / 65B / 70B / Falcon-40B.
TTFT is reduced by 85% / 61% / 87% / 86% compared with recomputation.
Cost savings are 70% / 43% / 66% / 68% compared with recomputation.
At 128 GB DRAM / 10 TB SSD, the hit rate is 86% for CachedAttention, 58% for LRU and 48% for FIFO.
Over 99.6% of CachedAttention's hits are DRAM hits.
The LRU and FIFO baselines in the placement ablation also lack prefetching, so the contributions of fetching and of eviction are not measured separately.
As the session arrival rate rises from 0.5 to 2.0/s (LLaMA-13B), the hit rate falls from 82% to 77%.
result.summary:
Short answer: AAS's real advantage over CachedAttention is one thing. It acts on sessions that are still in their gap, using time (seconds) and SSD-read backlog to decide when to fetch. CachedAttention (CA) only looks at jobs already in the queue, counts its window in jobs, and sizes it by capacity. Most other parts are either the same idea, inherited from SGLang, or not yet shown to beat CA.

**Where AAS stands out**
1. **Sessions in their gap (new relative to CA).**
   - CA fetches nothing and gives no eviction order for a session with no queued job.
   - In our runs, on average only about 11 of 128 sessions (x70) and 14 of 80 (campaign 10) were queued or running. So roughly 82-89% of cached sessions are invisible to a queue-only policy at any moment.
   - Today's fork already fetches when a request is enqueued, which is effectively CA's fetch trigger (the prefetch budget never filled at x70). Under it, 19.6% / 18.6% of returning turns at x70 were SSD restores, with mean TTFT 5.18 / 5.57 s.
   - 58-80% of that time was waiting behind other reads on one FIFO read thread. Meanwhile the SSD was idle 73-77% of the time, with 10-second demand bursts at about 2.1x its bandwidth. Only reads started before the turn arrives can move that burst into the idle time.
   - Simulated with true arrival times and earliest-deadline-first reads: a 10 s lead hides 81-91% of fetch time, and a 20 s lead cuts mean returning TTFT by 40% / 66%.
2. **Seconds instead of jobs, with backlog and bandwidth in the lead (extends CA).**
   - Leading by only a read's own transfer time hides 16-24%; the lead has to cover the queue of earlier reads.
   - Parking staged pages costs more the longer they wait: about 1% re-evicted at a 10 s lead, 56-64% at 60 s (model).
   - A capacity-sized window like CA's would park about 110 s of work at x1, close to one full L2 turnover.
3. **Page-level residency with a shared prefix (extends CA).**
   - Restores read only about 70% of each prompt, because the shared 7,808-token system prompt stays resident. Whole-session items would read about 1.4x the bytes on an already contended SSD.
   - Storing that shared prompt once per session would take about 61% of L2.
4. **Protection measured in seconds, eviction by predicted admission that also covers in-gap sessions, and an admission-time fallback** whose error cost is lopsided:
   - over-predicting the gap only falls back to today's behaviour;
   - history predictors keep 54-71% of the gain but add roughly 28-45% more SSD reads.
5. **Inclusion and write amplification.** About 40% of L2 mirrors GPU memory. CA never meets this problem because HBM is not a cache tier in its design.

**Where CA is the same or stronger**
- Same idea, already in SGLang: layer-wise host-to-GPU loading and asynchronous saving. The host-to-GPU path costs only about 0.04-0.08 s per host hit here.
- CA is stronger on:
  - context-overflow truncation (never exercised here: the largest prompt was 90.6K tokens against a 131K window);
  - disk-tier capacity management and TTL (our L3 never evicted, yet wrote about 725 GB in 2 hours);
  - implementation and end-to-end measurement (AAS exists only as oracle and model estimates).
- **The dense-regime gain (93-95% of prefill is recompute at x10/x1) is not evidence against CA.**
  - The fork lacks CA's own queue mechanisms (tail-first demotion and fetching for queued jobs) and upstream's admission-time SSD re-query (#39283).
  - Its LRU-refresh order evicts the request about to run next first, which is the opposite of CA's rule.
- **At realistic cadence (campaign 10) the headroom is small:** about 0.6 s on about 2.6% of turns, and every one of those restores followed a human pause of 7.7-33 minutes.

**Further improvements**
1. **Fair baselines before any claim.**
   - Build a CA-faithful baseline: job-count prefetch window, tail-first demotion, re-fetch for queued jobs.
   - Add a port of #39283.
   - Run both at x70, x10 and x1, plus ablations: earliest-deadline-first vs FIFO reads, and before-arrival vs queue-only fetching.
2. **Replace point prediction of the gap with hazard-based staging that uses idle SSD bandwidth**, bounded by the horizon H and the protection budget β.
   - Use the turn-end type: a tool call means the session returns in seconds; a reply waiting on the user means it will likely go cold. That signal can trigger early demotion.
   - Use a harness hint such as "user started typing": the 0.62 s fetch needs only about 1 s of lead.
3. **Skip SSD writes for pages L3 already holds.**
   - The write path never checks whether L3 has a page: unified_radix_cache.py:1632 → cache_controller.py:1266 → hicache_nixl.py:847. This is consistent with host writes equalling SSD writes exactly in every run.
   - At x1 this would remove most of the 58M rewritten tokens (about 0.6 GiB/s) and free that bandwidth for just-in-time reloads.
   - CA-style demote-on-evict would not help here: host evictions are about equal to write-through volume, and roughly 4x larger at x70 if disk copies are not kept.
4. **Add L3 drop and TTL keyed on predicted admission time**, CA's disk window translated to time.
5. **Ablate mirror reclaim first.** By the model it may shrink x70's SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5%, which would also shrink what the timing lever can address.
6. Add a pre-admission L2-to-GPU read buffer only if it is cheap; the gain is at most about 0.08 s per host hit.
7. Add positional-encoding-decoupled storage only if real agent traces overflow the window.
8. Re-run without the client connection cap, with several seeds, and fill the x20-x50 gap scales.

improvements.name: A. Working-set admission control to stop the dense-regime goodput collapse
improvements.idea: When the predicted live set (contexts of running plus queued sessions) exceeds unique L1+L2, admit only from an active set of sessions whose contexts fit. Order the active set by Â and use FCFS within it. Parked sessions may fall to L3. Rotate parked sessions in by age every quantum Q, or whenever an active session enters a long gap. A parked session's Â is its scheduled swap-in time, so AAS stages it from L3 just before its slot. This is Denning-style load control on top of AAS. Today AAS keeps FCFS and only stages and protects.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: Measured: completions per 300 s window from turns_three_tier_to.csv. x1: 4.49 turns/s with 6.9% of prompt tokens uncached in minutes 0-5; 1.70/s (14.6%) in 5-10; 0.67/s (62.4%) in 10-15; 0.21/s (78.6-79.1%) at 120-130 min. x10 has the same shape (4.44 -> 2.21 -> 0.59 -> 0.21/s). On the same 128 conversations, x70 sustained 1.2-3.2 turns/s with 1-9% uncached. Over the whole x1 run, 57.1M uncached tokens in 8,686 s is about 6.6K tok/s, close to the ~7.5K tok/s batched prefill rate, so the server spends most of its time recomputing. That makes this a metastable goodput collapse, not only a capacity limit. Campaign 10's hbm_lru collapses the same way at realistic cadence: queue wait 107 s, 100% recompute in the window. AAS alone cannot hold the x1 queue: 1.71-1.80M tokens of queued private context against at most 0.96M of host-only L2. The live set exceeds L1+L2 for 42-48% of the x10/x1 runs.
improvements.expected_gain: Estimate: if recompute falls back to x70 levels, x1/x10 throughput moves from 0.2-0.7 to at least ~1.4 turns/s (the x70 capacity implied by 1.18 turns/s being about 85%). That is 2-6x, and t95 completion would fall from ~7,790 s toward ~3,200 s. Mean TTFT in the 128-session closed loop is set by Little's law (128 / throughput, minus decode, minus gap), so it falls only to ~50-85 s from 131 s. The prize is throughput and session makespan. Parked sessions pay a bounded extra wait.
improvements.cost_and_risk: Unfairness and starvation for parked sessions: it needs an aging bound and a fairness metric. Q and the active-set size are new knobs. If the estimate of unique L1+L2 is wrong, the system either still thrashes or leaves capacity idle. LPM silently falls back to FCFS above 128 waiting requests (schedule_policy.py:295), so the policy has to be explicit, not layered on lpm. The closed-loop client may overstate the gain (see J).
improvements.prior_work_overlap: Denning's working-set model and load control (virtual-memory thrashing). Autellix (program-level scheduling for agents). Continuum (program-aware scheduling with KV TTL). SGLang lpm (cache-aware order, falls back to FCFS above 128 waiting). Strata-style deferral, as named in our design notes. CachedAttention takes the scheduler as given and only reads the queue; it never reorders jobs by cache location. As far as I found, none of these combines load control with timed SSD swap-in of parked sessions.
improvements.how_to_test: x1 and x10 with the client connection cap removed: ARMS="three_tier_wc three_tier_wc_ws" LEVEL=NAT160 MODEL=Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 CTX=131072 KV_DTYPE=auto TRACE=/sgl-workspace/sglang/agent_cache/traces/lmcache_agentic_trace_262k.json NCONV=128 C=128 TURNS=40 OFFSET=32 GAP=1 (then GAP=10) GAP_CAP=1200 bash agent_cache/scripts/run_compare.sh. three_tier_wc_ws is a new start_server.sh arm. Compare against B0, lpm (B8) and the #39283 re-query port (B3). Report throughput and uncached share per 300 s window, session makespan p50/p95, per-session maximum TTFT and Jain's fairness index. Gate: uncached share stays under 10% after minute 10, and throughput is at least 2x B3.

improvements.name: B. Non-inclusive L2 for running requests: copy to host at request finish, not at prefill end
improvements.idea: Move the D2H write-through of a request's prompt pages from the last prefill chunk to request finish. The pages stay device-locked until the copy acks, as pending write-throughs already do. The SSD write is chained after that copy. While a request decodes, its context lives in L1 (and in L3 if it was written earlier), so L2 holds only queued and idle contexts. Together with element 9 (idle-mirror reclaim), L1/L2 becomes fully non-inclusive without write_back's synchronous D2H.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: About 39-40% of L2 (636-656K tokens) mirrors L1 in every run. The idle mirror is only 3.0% of L2 at x1 and 5.9-6.7% at x10, so ~33-36% of L2 (~540-590K tokens) mirrors contexts that are running and device-locked. Those copies sit unused for a whole decode: decode_mean is 53.5 s (x1), 50.5 s (x10) and 10.3 s (x70) in crossscale.csv. 72-98% of write volume is triggered at the last prefill chunk. At x1, queued private context is 1.71-1.80M against at most 0.96M of host-only L2; adding ~0.55M gives ~1.5M, close to the ~1.59M needed to hold the whole queue. Measured H2D runs at ~32-35 GB/s (about 19.8K tokens in p50 54-64 ms), so a finish-time copy costs ~60 ms of PCIe per context, off the critical path.
improvements.expected_gain: +0.54-0.59M tokens for queued contexts at x10/x1: +33-36% of L2, or about +60% of host-only space. About +10% of L2 at x70 (total mirror 39-40% minus idle mirror 29-31%). Combined with Â-ordered eviction, it could hold most of the x1 queue in L2. That removes most just-in-time L3 reloads, which would exceed SSD bandwidth at a healthy admission rate.
improvements.cost_and_risk: A decoding request that is retracted or preempted has no host copy and must recompute; retraction counts are not yet measured. Finish-time D2H bursts compete with H2D loads. Finished nodes stay device-locked a little longer while their copy is pending. write_through_threshold semantics change. The SSD copy is delayed by the decode time, which matters only for crash recovery.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: This is the opposite of CachedAttention's asynchronous saving. CA writes prefill KV layer by layer during decoding and decode KV while decoding, to keep saving off the critical path, and its HBM is not a cross-turn cache tier. Our L1 is a cache tier (96% GPU hits for gaps under 1 min in campaign 10), so early copies only duplicate. The existing extremes in SGLang are write_back (synchronous D2H at eviction, ~50x the per-token cost) and buffer_only host mode (L2 as a staging buffer only). Design element 9 covers only idle mirrors.
improvements.how_to_test: x1 and x10 arms: three_tier_wc vs three_tier_wc + finish-copy (with and without element 9) vs write_back (B7). Metrics: mirror size, host-only L2 occupancy, rate of admissions with only the shared prompt cached, recompute share, admissions/s, retraction count. Rerun x70 and campaign 10 to check there is no regression in host hits (campaign 10, 1-5 min class: 92.5% host).

improvements.name: C. Deduplicate L3 writes (skip pages the SSD already holds)
improvements.idea: Before backing a node up to L3, drop the pages whose hash L3 already has. Either call batch_exists in the backup thread, or keep an in-memory set or Bloom filter of acked keys (L3 is wiped at boot and has a single writer in these runs) that the L3 cleaner invalidates. The file and Mooncake backends already behave this way.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: nixl batch_set_v1 writes every page unconditionally (python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage/nixl/hicache_nixl.py:847-876). HiCacheFile skips existing keys (hicache_storage.py:521-525) and Mooncake's batch_set_v1 checks existence. On the same 128 conversations, x70 wc wrote 3.57M tokens, roughly the unique content (0 cold returns). x1 wrote 57.97M and x10 53.92M (d2h = h2s), so ~54.4M and ~50.3M tokens (~94%) are rewrites: about 5.35 and 4.95 TB per run, ~0.6 GB/s at x1. At x70 the to arm wrote 5.27M against wc's 3.57M, so 1.7M tokens (32% of its writes) are rewrites after aborted reads and recomputes. In x70 to, reads overlapping at least 0.3 GiB/s of write-through ran at p50 1.36 GiB/s (n=174), against 3.31 GiB/s with no concurrent writes (n=310).
improvements.expected_gain: SSD writes drop by 90% or more at x10/x1 and ~30% in the x70 to arm. Endurance improves (about 5.3 TB per x1 run down to ~0.35 TB), and read bandwidth is freed during restore bursts. On its own this does not change dense-regime TTFT, since recompute stays; it removes the write side of the self-reinforcing loop.
improvements.cost_and_risk: One extra metadata query per backup batch; existence queries measured p50 1 ms. A positive can go stale if the cleaner or another instance deletes the key between the check and its use, so it needs a cleaner hook, or a backend-side check when L3 is shared by several writers.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: SGLang's file and Mooncake backends already skip existing keys; LMCache deduplicates by chunk hash. CachedAttention reaches disk only by demotion, never write-through, so (my inference) this rewrite problem does not arise there.
improvements.how_to_test: x1 (GAP=1, same settings as A): three_tier_to vs three_tier_to_dedup. iostat wkB/s on /dev/vdc should fall to x70-like levels while h2s submits stay the same. At x70 (GAP=70 GAP_CAP=1200), compare the s2h_io GiB/s distribution and timeout aborts (64 in B0). As a unit check, replay one conversation twice and assert the bytes are written once.

improvements.name: D. Give restores priority over write-through on the SSD
improvements.idea: Treat L3 writes as background work with slack: a page's deadline is its predicted L2 eviction. Pause or throttle the backup thread while a read with a near deadline is queued or running. Bound the host bytes not yet backed to L3, so eviction never waits on a write.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: Per-read bandwidth in x70 to (s2h_io reads over 4K tokens), binned by concurrent write-through: p50 3.31 GiB/s under 0.05 GiB/s of writes (n=310), 1.89 at 0.05-0.3 (n=409), 1.36 at 0.3 GiB/s or more (n=174). Campaign 10 to: 3.30 -> 3.08 -> 2.64 (n=9) -> 1.39 (n=1). The wc arm shows little effect (2.00 / 1.89 / 2.10, with only 16 reads under heavy writes). This is correlational, not a controlled test. O_DIRECT was active, so the page cache does not explain it. In campaign 7 iostat, the 10-s peak read rate was 2.03 GiB/s at an average queue size of ~112. Writes have slack: L2 turns over in ~131-145 s at x10/x1 and in minutes at x70.
improvements.expected_gain: If the interference is causal, restore IO during x70 bursts falls ~30-60% (own IO is 0.82-0.90 s on average), and the lead time element 3 needs shrinks. Little effect at campaign-10 load (SSD at most 34% busy).
improvements.cost_and_risk: Host pages stay locked longer while their L3 write waits, which adds L2 pressure and interacts with the backup-skip path (unified_radix_cache.py:1410-1414). Starved writes must be force-flushed before L2 eviction. A controlled fio test should come first.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: Classic read-over-write IO scheduling (deadline/mq-deadline, writeback throttling). Design element 3 paces reads plus write-through under BW but does not give reads priority. CachedAttention migrates host-to-disk on separate IO threads, only by eviction, and its windows ignore disk bandwidth.
improvements.how_to_test: First fio on /dev/vdc with O_DIRECT: 2 MiB sequential reads alone, then with 0.3 / 0.6 / 1.0 GiB/s of concurrent writes. Then x70 (GAP=70 GAP_CAP=1200 NCONV=128 C=128 TURNS=40 OFFSET=32): three_tier_wc vs + write gating. Metrics: s2h_io GiB/s by concurrent-write bin, storage-hit TTFT p50/p90, h2s lag, peak unbacked host bytes.

improvements.name: E. Backlog-aware compute-or-load (or split) instead of the timeout abort
improvements.idea: At fetch issue, and again at admission, compare the expected load completion ((EDF backlog + own bytes) / BW) with recompute time at the current prefill throughput. Recompute when that is cheaper and the GPU has headroom; otherwise load. Or split the work Cake-style: recompute the first x tokens while loading the rest from the back, choosing x so both finish together (x / r_gpu = (n - x) / r_ssd). This replaces the timeout policy's wait-then-abort.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: x70 to: 64 reads (98 GiB) were aborted after a mean 7.42 s wait, and those turns then recomputed at 10.41 s mean TTFT, paying for both. Storage-hit wait behind other reads averages 3.01 s (to) and 4.43 s (wc), against 0.82-0.90 s of own IO. A restore is ~20.3K tokens. Single-request recompute runs at about 4,903 tok/s (~4.1 s for a restore). Per-read SSD p50 is 1.89-3.31 GiB/s, about 20.6K-36.2K tok/s. Arithmetic: uncontended, a split takes 0.79 s against 0.98 s for load alone (-19%). Behind a 3.0 s backlog it takes ~3.2 s against 4.0 s. Behind a 4.4 s backlog, recompute alone (4.1 s) wins. In a healthy dense regime the restore demand is several GB/s, above what the SSD delivers; GPU recompute adds ~7.5K tok/s of restore capacity (+20-35%).
improvements.expected_gain: Removes the 64 doubly-paid turns (~5-6 s each) in x70 to. Under backlog, storage-hit TTFT is capped near recompute time. It also gives a principled fallback for mispredicted arrivals and for the dense regime once it is SSD-bound.
improvements.cost_and_risk: Recompute takes GPU time from decode and other prefills (x70 was offered ~85% of capacity), so the cost model must use live throughput and can oscillate. The split needs loading of a suffix page range plus prefill of a prefix in the radix tree, which is not trivial plumbing.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: Cake (compute or load, bidirectional); InferCept (cost model for preserve, discard or swap around tool calls); optional baseline B9 in our evaluation plan. CachedAttention does not say what happens when a job reaches the queue head while its KV is still on disk, and has no recompute fallback or backlog model.
improvements.how_to_test: x70: three_tier_to (B0) vs a new three_tier_cost arm, plus a run with the SSD throttled to 0.5x (cgroup io.max on /dev/vdc), as in the evaluation plan. Metrics: aborted reads, storage-hit TTFT p50/p90, GPU prefill-time share, total recomputed tokens.

improvements.name: F. Remove the ~35 ms admission delay from the arrival-time L3 query (cause of the unexplained SSD-tier p50 cost)
improvements.idea: When the L3 existence query for a request's unmatched suffix returns 0 hits, make the request admissible in the same scheduling pass: either wait synchronously for the query (p99 3 ms) or re-check prefetch progress right after check_hicache_events. Skip the query entirely when the session registry shows the suffix starts past the session's last committed length: freshly produced tool output cannot be on L3.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: Measured from campaign 10 ReqTimeStats. In both SSD arms, requests whose unmatched suffix is at least 256 tokens (prefetch_threshold) wait p50 36.6 ms / p90 54 ms in the server queue. Requests with a suffix under 256 wait 1.0-1.2 ms, as do all requests in hbm_host. Paired against hbm_host: +34.6 ms (n=5,331) vs -0.1 / 0.0 ms (n≈4,025). The query itself takes p50 1 ms (s2h_query minus prefetch_start, 5,313 zero-hit queries), so the delay is the request waiting for a later scheduling pass. This explains the +0.02 s paired p50 cost of the SSD tier: for suffixes of 256 or more, device-hit p50 TTFT is 0.332 s (to) vs 0.292 s (hbm_host); for suffixes under 256 both are 0.231 s. It affects 55.9% of returning turns in campaign 10 and 55-56% at x70.
improvements.expected_gain: -35 ms on ~57% of requests at realistic cadence. Mean returning TTFT goes from ~0.351 to ~0.33 s (about -6%), and p50 for the affected device hits drops ~11%. This removes the only cost of the SSD tier measured so far.
improvements.cost_and_risk: A synchronous wait adds at most ~3 ms per query batch to the scheduler loop. The registry skip could miss a real L3 hit for identical content under the same prefix in a forked session, which is rare. Low risk.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: None; this is an implementation defect in arrival-time prefetch. It is unrelated to CachedAttention.
improvements.how_to_test: Campaign-10 cadence: TRACE=/sgl-workspace/sglang/agent_cache/traces/lmcache_agentic_trace_262k_ge45_tl_s1.json NCONV=283 C=80 TURNS=50 GAP=1 GAP_CAP=0 ARRIVAL=0.1 CLIENT_TIMEOUT=7200, comparing three_tier_wc with three_tier_wc + fix. A quick diagnostic needs no code: set a large "prefetch_threshold" in l3_extra.json (it is parsed from hicache_storage_backend_extra_config) and check that queue_duration for suffixes of 256 or more drops to ~1 ms; that arm loses real restores. Metrics: ReqTimeStats queue_duration by suffix bin, and TTFT paired against hbm_host.

improvements.name: G. Human-pause staging from a client return-intent hint and the turn-end type, not from duration prediction
improvements.idea: Do not try to predict how long a human pauses; get the lead time from the client. (1) At turn end, record whether the reply hands control to the human (no tool call) or calls a tool; this is a binary class known at turn end. Use it in the Â key: sessions waiting on a human are ranked by survival of the pause distribution, sessions waiting on a tool count as near-term. (2) Add a lightweight warm(session) hint that the client sends when the user starts typing or focuses the session. It stages the session's registry chain from L3 to L2 and protects it for H. With an uncontended SSD the lead needed is only ~0.6 s plus a margin.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: Campaign 10: all 185 SSD restores followed gaps of 459-1,992 s (p50 1,306 s). SSD share by gap: 450-600 s 16/31, 600-900 s 37/44, 900-1,800 s 66/68, 1,800 s or more 66/66, so L2 keeps an idle session ~8-10 min. The trace's think pause is lognormal with p50 84 s and p90 1,236 s (sigma ≈ 2.1, p90/p50 ≈ 15x) and is drawn independently of the reply, so no history or quantile predictor can land inside a ±10 s window. The restore fetch is ~0.58 s (s2h_io mean, n=179) of a 1.01 s TTFT. Removing 0.58 s from each restored turn: whole-arm returning mean 0.351 -> 0.339 s, p99 1.363 -> 1.214 s.
improvements.expected_gain: Restored turns go from 1.01 to ~0.43 s (-0.58 s on 2.0-2.6% of returning turns): -11% p99 and -3% mean at campaign-10 cadence. This is the turn the user sees right after coming back. The gain is larger when the SSD is contended, for example many users returning together after a meeting.
improvements.cost_and_risk: Needs API and client changes. Spurious hints waste SSD reads (~1.9 GB each), so hints need a per-session rate limit and protection must be dropped if no request follows within H. The replay's pauses are synthetic, so the turn-end class can only be emulated as an oracle flag.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: Ask the Tool (lead time from a tool's live progress); TokenCake (per-function duration estimates); SYMPHONY (client advisories, including expected arrival); Continuum (TTL by tool type). None of the sources examined uses a signal that human input has started. CachedAttention treats returning requests as arriving randomly and has no model of think time.
improvements.how_to_test: Campaign-10 cadence (as in F). replay_agentic.py sends the hint T_lead ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 5 s} before any turn with gap_think > 0, plus the class flag at the previous turn's end. Arms: three_tier_wc vs + hint. Metrics: TTFT in the 10-min-or-longer gap class and SSD read amplification. Add a stress variant with synchronized human returns (e.g. 40 sessions returning within 30 s) to cover the contended case.

improvements.name: H. Evict from the queue tail first (removing the arrival-time refresh is not enough)
improvements.idea: Implement element 6 as a new EvictionStrategy whose priority reads Â from the session registry. Queued sessions are ordered by FCFS position, tail evicted first. In-gap sessions are ordered by predicted return. Plain LRU applies only to nodes no session owns. Also stop refreshing last_access_time on arrival-time matches of queued requests and on lpm's per-pass matches.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: At x1 the inter-turn gap is p50 0.70 s while server wait is p10/p50/p90 6.7 / 111 / 255 s. So finish order ≈ arrival order ≈ admission order, and plain LRU without the refresh would still evict the queue head (the oldest finish) first; dropping the refresh alone does not fix the order. The existing priority policy keys on node.priority, which is the maximum over all requests ever (unified_tree_core.py:953, 1041). Because it never decreases, it cannot carry a dynamic Â. Loss vs wait at x1: 0% under 10 s, 29-35% at 20-30 s, 94% or more beyond 60 s.
improvements.expected_gain: Upper bound: the 49-55% of returns admitted with only the shared prompt cached (93-95% of prefill). The achievable share is limited by how much of the queue L2 can hold (at most 0.96M host-only vs 1.71-1.80M queued) unless combined with B. It is also the cheapest test of the Â idea, since it needs no predictor.
improvements.cost_and_risk: In sparse regimes queue position carries little information, so the key must fall back to LRU or Â. Interacts with the protection budget. In the closed loop, the tail's restore is delayed, but the tail is admitted last anyway.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: CachedAttention demotes from host to disk starting at the tail of its look-ahead window, using queue position as future-access information, but leaves the order among sessions with no queued job unspecified. Our Â also covers sessions still in their gap. Related: PCR's look-ahead LRU; Belady.
improvements.how_to_test: Step 1(c) of the evaluation plan, at x10 and x1: three_tier_wc vs + tail-first key. Add a no-refresh-only arm to confirm it does not help on its own. Metrics: rate of admissions with only the shared prompt cached, the loss-vs-wait curve, recompute share.

improvements.name: I. Session-aware L3 capacity management (TTL from pause survival, garbage-collect ended sessions)
improvements.idea: Bound L3 and evict by session state: ended sessions first (client close or final turn), then sessions whose probability of returning within the horizon is below ε given idle time so far and turn-end class, then LRU. Exempt sessions whose Â is within a window, the way CachedAttention exempts queued jobs.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: L3 was effectively unbounded: the 70/60% cleaner never fired and there were 0 cleanups. Campaign 10 wrote ~725 GB per SSD arm and left a ~676 GB store, with at most 80 of 233 conversations still live (about 66% finished; the byte share was not measured). 2.7% of replies are final turns. The trace caps human pauses at 30 min; real users can return hours later.
improvements.expected_gain: Estimate: the L3 footprint tracks the live set (80 sessions × ~2-4 GB) instead of every context ever written, about 2-3x less SSD capacity at campaign-10 load. It also stops a capacity-driven LRU cleaner from dropping sessions that are about to return.
improvements.cost_and_risk: A wrong ended signal turns a 1.0 s restore into a 3.2 s recompute (campaign 10, returns after 10 min or more). Needs a session-close API and TTL tuning.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: CachedAttention gives each session a TTL measured from its last access (1 h in its capacity experiment) and has a look-ahead eviction window that exempts queued jobs from being dropped out of AttentionStore. Also related: the file backend's LRU evictor and LMCache TTL.
improvements.how_to_test: Campaign-10 cadence with L3 capped (e.g. ~300 GB through L3_CLEANER_PCT and a size quota on /mnt/ssd/hicache_l3): stock cleaner vs session-aware cleaner, with the replay marking conversation end. Metrics: tier shares in the 10-min-or-longer class (SSD vs recompute), bytes the cleaner deletes, SSD hit rate.

improvements.name: J. Evaluate the dense regime open-loop, on goodput
improvements.idea: Reproduce x10/x1-like density with open-loop session arrivals (Poisson) at 50-120% of capacity. Report admissions/s and recompute share over time, plus session makespan, rather than closed-loop mean TTFT. Use the same setup to map the x70 -> x10 transition.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: With 128 closed-loop sessions, mean TTFT ≈ 128 / throughput, minus decode, minus gap. Even at the x70 capacity (~1.4 turns/s), x1 TTFT would be ~70-85 s, so TTFT cannot reveal a fix for the collapse; throughput can (0.21-0.67 vs ~1.4 turns/s or more). replay_agentic.py already has --arrival-rate (campaign 10 used 0.1 sessions/s with C=80). The x10/x1 runs were also shaped by the 100-connection cap (since fixed), and nothing has been run between x10 and x70.
improvements.expected_gain: Valid measurement of the dense-regime claim. It also shows the load at which the collapse starts for B0, B3 and AAS.
improvements.cost_and_risk: Longer runs. Open-loop arrivals above capacity diverge, so runs need CLIENT_TIMEOUT. A capacity estimate is needed first.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: CachedAttention generated Poisson session arrivals (λ = 1.0/s by default, swept 0.5-2.0/s) but modelled no think time between turns. Our closed loop has gaps but no control over arrival rate.
improvements.how_to_test: ARRIVAL ∈ {0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08} sessions/s with a large C (e.g. 256) on the 262K trace at GAP=1/10/70 via run_compare.sh. Plot throughput and uncached share per 300 s window and find the knee for B0, B3, AAS and A.

improvements.name: K. Chunk-level EDF on the single read lane (not more read threads)
improvements.idea: Keep one read lane, but split each restore into page batches (STORAGE_BATCH_SIZE) and choose the next batch by earliest Â. A read close to its deadline can then overtake a 2 GB read already in progress. A request is admitted only when all its pages have landed.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: In campaign 7 iostat, the single nixl read thread already reached the device's 10-s peak (2.03 GiB/s at an average queue size of ~112), so more threads would add no bandwidth. Reads are strictly serial (s2h_io overlaps 4/960 and 0/837). Each restore holds the lane for ~0.6-1.0 s (~2 GB). 10-s demand peaks reach 2.1x the SSD's bandwidth, and hits arriving at queue depth 5 or more carry 72-81% of fetch-window time.
improvements.expected_gain: A refinement of element 3. It helps when deadlines are tight relative to one read (unpredicted arrivals, dense staging). With 10-20 s leads it is likely small over request-level EDF.
improvements.cost_and_risk: Scheduling overhead per batch. Large restores can be repeatedly overtaken. A preempted partial read holds its host pages longer.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: Design element 3 (EDF per request); deadline disk schedulers; py-kvcache's preloads that yield to demand loads. CachedAttention sizes its windows by capacity, not by time or disk bandwidth.
improvements.how_to_test: x70 (to and wc) with oracle Â taken from the replay: request-level EDF vs chunk-level EDF. Metrics: deadline misses (fetch finished after admission), storage-hit p90.

improvements.name: L. Pre-load the next admissions into L1 (CachedAttention read-buffer analog), low priority
improvements.idea: SGLang already overlaps the L2->L1 load layer by layer with the forward pass (LayerDoneCounter at cache_controller.py:71-96; per-layer wait at memory_pool.py:1425-1426), which is the first half of CachedAttention's layer-wise pre-loading. The missing half is CA's read buffer: start the H2D load for the 1-2 requests with the earliest Â while the previous batch runs, into a small reserved region of L1.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: H2D of ~19.8K tokens takes p50 54-64 ms (32-35 GB/s). Host-hit minus device-hit p50 TTFT, with matched suffix: campaign 10 hbm_host +52 ms (suffix under 256) / +84 ms (256-2048); campaign 10 three_tier_to +26 / +40 ms; x70 wc -25 / -1 ms. Host hits are 9-10% of returning turns in campaign 10 and ~40% at x70.
improvements.expected_gain: At most ~30-80 ms on host-hit turns; under 1% on mean returning TTFT at campaign-10 cadence.
improvements.cost_and_risk: Reserving L1 shrinks batch capacity, and L1 is the binding resource in the dense regime. Loads are wasted if Â slips.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: CachedAttention's layer-wise pre-loading with an HBM read buffer: on LLaMA-13B with 1K history + 100 new tokens, prefill time fell 35% with no buffer (PL-B0) and 61% with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15). SGLang HiCache's layer-wise load-back already covers the overlap part.
improvements.how_to_test: Campaign 10 and x70: three_tier_wc vs + head staging. Metrics: host-tier TTFT p50 by suffix bin, L1 batch size, decode throughput.

improvements.name: M. Â-aware session-affinity routing for several instances sharing L3
improvements.idea: Route each returning turn to the instance that holds its context in L1/L2, unless that instance's predicted admission delay costs more than restoring from the shared L3 elsewhere (or recomputing). Feed each instance's Â and backlog to the router. After a reroute, stage the context at the target with AAS.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: No multi-instance data: the testbed is a single H200. Campaign-10 TTFT by tier: GPU 0.355 s (gaps under 1 min), host 0.39 s (1-5 min), SSD 1.02 s, recompute 3.21 s. A misrouted short-gap turn therefore costs ~0.65 s with a shared L3 and ~2.9 s without one. x70 queues reached 73-79, so affinity alone can overload one instance.
improvements.expected_gain: Unknown. Bounded by the per-tier costs above times the misroute rate.
improvements.cost_and_risk: The router needs per-instance cache state; load imbalance; contention on the shared L3 grows with the number of instances.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: SGLang's cache-aware router, NVIDIA Dynamo's KV-aware routing, Mooncake's KV-centric scheduler, Preble, Autellix's locality-aware load balancing. CachedAttention does not discuss multi-instance routing.
improvements.how_to_test: First a trace-driven simulator using the campaign-10 per-tier latencies and registry residency, comparing round-robin, sticky and Â-aware routing. Then two instances on one nixl L3 directory if a second GPU is available.

improvements.name: N. Invalidate on compaction or divergence; defer position-decoupled KV
improvements.idea: When a session's new prompt diverges from its registry chain well below n_s (compaction, history edit, rewind), mark the orphaned chain evict-first in L1/L2 and delete it from L3. Do not invest in RoPE-decoupled KV storage until a trace with compaction shows reuse of shifted segments.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: The 262K trace has 0 context-shrink events in 24,111 turn pairs, and final prompts reach at most 104K tokens against CTX 131,072, so CachedAttention-style overflow truncation never triggers in our data. 16.8% of the text in messages of at least 400 characters at turn 1 or later (7.3M of 43.6M chars) repeats verbatim in another conversation at a different position. These are new delta tokens, though (campaign 10 averages ~550 uncached tokens per returning turn), so position-independent reuse would save at most ~100 prefill tokens per turn. The duplicate share may be inflated by several agents running the same SWE-bench task.
improvements.expected_gain: Each compaction frees ~n_s tokens of L2 and L3; how often real agents compact is unknown (zero in our trace). Position decoupling gives a negligible gain on our workloads.
improvements.cost_and_risk: A fork the user later returns to could be misread as dead. Position decoupling would need pre-RoPE K storage, RoPE applied at load in the attention backends, and accuracy checks.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: CachedAttention's positional-encoding-decoupled truncation: it stores K/V before RoPE and requires relative position encoding. With truncation ratio 0.5, its hit rate beat the OF baseline by 17.6-41.5 points. Its token-discarding-list hook is described but not evaluated. CacheBlend and EPIC do position-independent reuse.
improvements.how_to_test: Build a compaction variant of the trace with make_tl_trace.py: replace the history with a ~2K-token summary once the context passes, say, 40K tokens. Run it at campaign-10 cadence. Metrics: orphaned bytes resident in L2/L3 over time, how long they take to be evicted, and TTFT of the turn after compaction.

improvements.name: O. Keep eviction session-atomic under the new Â key
improvements.idea: When eviction moves from LRU to Â order, evict one session's whole private chain before touching another session's pages, as CachedAttention does with whole-session items. A restore pays the SSD read latency for any missing tail, so spreading evictions over many sessions' tails multiplies the number of sessions that need L3 reads.
improvements.evidence_from_our_data: Today's radix LRU is already session-atomic in practice. SSD restores that also had at least 1K host tokens: 1 of 890 (x70 to), 6 of 837 (x70 wc), 4 of 185 (campaign 10). Restores average 19-20.5K storage tokens plus the 7.8K shared prompt on device. An Â key with per-node ties or bucketed predictions could interleave tails from different sessions.
improvements.expected_gain: Keeps the number of SSD-restored sessions minimal for a given amount of eviction, and avoids a regression when element 6 is introduced.
improvements.cost_and_risk: Session-atomic eviction can over-evict when only a small amount of space is needed (evict a whole 20K chain to free 2K). Shared prefixes must stay excluded.
improvements.prior_work_overlap: CachedAttention's minimal eviction and fetch unit is one whole session, because a session's KV is either all used or none of it is used.
improvements.how_to_test: In every element-6 ablation, log restores that mix host and storage tokens and the number of distinct sessions touched per evict_host call. Gate: mixed restores stay under ~2%.

ca_claims: CachedAttention (USENIX ATC '24; arXiv 2403.19708 v3) overlaps loading of historical KV from host memory to HBM with the prefill of new tokens, layer by layer (layer-wise pre-loading).

CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer so pre-loading can start while the previous job is still running, and sizes it as Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew); imperfect overlap occurs when Tload·Lhist > Tpref·Lnew.

In CachedAttention's micro-benchmark (LLaMA-13B, 1K history + 100 new tokens), layer-wise pre-loading without a read buffer (PL-B0) reduced prefill time by 35%, and with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15) by 61%.

CachedAttention saves KV from HBM to host memory asynchronously: prefill KV is written layer by layer and overlapped with decoding, decode KV is written layer by layer while decoding, and unfinished writes go to a reserved HBM write buffer so the next job is not blocked.
CachedAttention rejects writing all KV after the turn ends because the saving time would be on the critical path, and reports that asynchronous saving cut total execution time by 13-15%.
In CachedAttention, HBM holds the execution buffer plus read and write buffers and is not used as a cross-turn cache tier; keeping KV in HBM only is evaluated as a baseline.
In CachedAttention, KV reaches disk by eviction (demotion) from host memory, triggered when free host memory reaches a threshold whose value is not given, not by write-through.
CachedAttention moves data between GPU and host on dedicated CUDA streams and between host memory and disks on separate IO threads.

CachedAttention prefetches KV from disk to host memory only for jobs already in the scheduler's queue, within a look-ahead window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs; nothing is fetched for a session with no queued job.

CachedAttention does not predict when a session's next turn will arrive and does not model think time between turns; the paper says that because conversation requests arrive randomly, their KV caches are more likely to be on disk when accessed.

CachedAttention's look-ahead eviction window, (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs long, exempts items whose job lies in the window from being evicted out of AttentionStore, and when demoting from host memory to disk it gives priority to items near the window's tail.
CachedAttention does not specify the eviction order among cached sessions that have no queued job.
CachedAttention's minimal eviction and fetching granularity is one item holding all the KV of a conversation session, because a session's KV is either all used or none of it is used.
CachedAttention's window lengths are derived from capacity, counted in jobs, and take no account of time, disk bandwidth or read backlog.
CachedAttention takes the scheduler as given and only reads its job queue; it does not reorder jobs by cache location and does not discuss preemption, priorities, SLOs or multi-instance routing.
CachedAttention does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk or being fetched (stall, recompute, or direct load).
CachedAttention gives each session's KV a TTL measured from its last access, set to one hour in its capacity experiment; the paper does not say how the TTL interacts with the eviction windows.

CachedAttention stores K and V before the relative positional encoding is applied, so that on context overflow the stored KV can be truncated and new positions applied after loading; this requires relative positional encoding.

CachedAttention evaluates truncation with a ratio of 0.5, and its hit rate exceeded the OF baseline (positions kept embedded, so overflow invalidates the cache) by 17.6, 41.5, 18.1 and 18.4 points for LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-65B, LLaMA-70B and Falcon-40B.
CachedAttention describes a token-discarding-list (TDL) hook for KV compression methods, but does not evaluate it.

CachedAttention generates session arrivals with a Poisson process (λ = 1.0 sessions/s by default, swept from 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s) on ShareGPT conversations, because the dataset has no arrival timestamps.

checks.claim: Layer-wise pre-loading overlaps loading the KV of later layers from host memory with the computation of the current layer.
checks.correction: Correct. The paper adds that the computation being overlapped is the prefill of the session's new input tokens: 'overlap the loading of the KV cache with the prefilling computation of new input tokens for the conversation.' Checked against arXiv v3, the ATC'24 camera-ready ('Accepted to USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2024'). The same wording is in v1.
checks.quote: "The main idea is to overlap the loading of the KV cache with the prefilling computation of new input tokens for the conversation. In particular, the LLM model is chained by multiple transformer layers, each with its own KV cache. As the GPU executes a layer, the KV cache needed by the subsequent layers can be loaded from the host memory concurrently. By doing so, when the GPU starts computing the self-attention for a layer, the corresponding KV cache of the layer is already in the HBM execution buffer."
checks.section: §3.2.1 Layer-wise Pre-loading from Memory to HBMs (Fig. 6b)

checks.claim: An HBM read buffer lets pre-loading start while the previous job is still running.
checks.correction: Correct. The stated reason: without the read buffer, loading cannot start until the previous job frees the HBM execution buffer, which leaves a gap before Layer 1. The read buffer removes that gap.
checks.quote: "However, a gap still exists between the last job and the first layer of the current job, since the loading can only commence once the HBM execution buffer is available, i.e., the last job is finished. To further mitigate the gap between the last job and the first layer of the current job, CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap. Specifically, as shown in Figure 6c, with the read buffer, the read stream doesn't have to wait for the release of the execution buffer from the last job. The read stream can start the pre-loading while the last job is running."

checks.claim: The read-buffer size is set by Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew).
checks.correction: The formula is quoted correctly.
