Definitions: Tload is the KV access time per token, Tpref is the prefill time per token, Lhist is the number of history tokens, Lnew is the number of new input tokens, and B is the PCIe bandwidth. The formula only applies under imperfect overlap (Tload·Lhist > Tpref·Lnew). Here the paper motivates a 'customized larger pre-loading buffer' that lets loading start earlier. Some of the paper's text calls it the 'buffer' or 'pre-loading buffer' rather than 'read buffer', though the evaluation labels these sizes as read-buffer sizes.
checks.quote: "Let Tload , Tpref, Lhist and Lnew denote the access time of the KV cache for a token, the prefilling time for a token, the length of historical tokens in a session, and the length of new input tokens in the conversation, respectively. Imperfect overlapping happens when Tload Lhist > Tpref Lnew, which indicates that the transmission time is larger than the partial prefilling time. The buffer is used to fill up the time gap Tload Lhist− Tpref Lnew. Combined with the PCIe bandwidth B, the buffer size can be set by the following formula: Sbuf = B(Tload Lhist− Tpref Lnew)."

checks.claim: With LLaMA-13B, 1K history plus 100 new tokens, pre-loading cuts prefill time by 35% with no read buffer (PL-B0) and by 61% with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15).
checks.correction: The numbers and setup are correct. Missing context: both reductions are measured against NO-PL (no pre-loading), on a single GPU with batch size 16. The paper also says the 15-layer buffer 'perfectly overlaps' the load time. The buffer is measured in layers of KV cache. The paper's text typos the label as 'PF-B15'; Fig. 19 labels it 'PL-B15'.
checks.quote: "The model used is LLaMA-13B with a single GPU and the batch size is set to 16. Layer-wise KV cache pre-loading. We set the length of historical tokens to 1K and the length of newly input tokens to 100 ... For clarity, we use the number of layers to represent the buffer size, e.g., PL-B0 indicates no read buffer and PF-B5 indicates a read buffer size of 5 layers of KV cache. We observe although there is no read buffer, i.e., PL-B0, the pre-loading scheme reduces the prefilling time by 35% compared to NO-PL. PF-B15 perfectly overlaps the KV cache loading time and reduces the prefilling time by 61% compared to NO-PL."
checks.section: §4.3.2 Overlapped KV cache Access (Fig. 19)

checks.claim: Asynchronous saving writes prefill-phase KV layer by layer, overlapped with decoding, writes decode-phase KV layer by layer while decoding, and moves unfinished writes to an HBM write buffer.
checks.correction: Accurate in substance. Wording differences: for prefill, the paper says the write stream 'retains' the KV layer by layer, and that this KV 'can be overlapped with' decoding. It does not literally say 'writes'. The write buffer is described as covering the case where write-back has not finished when decoding finishes, so that the next job is not blocked. The baseline it replaces writes all KV together after the round of conversation ends.
checks.quote: "As shown in Figure 8b, for the prefilling phase, as each self-attention operation can produce a significant amount of KV cache, the write stream retains the KV cache layer by layer. The KV cache produced by the prefilling phase can be overlapped with the decoding phase. For the decoding phase, as the KV cache is iteratively produced, the write stream writes back the KV cache layer by layer while decoding. To avoid getting stuck if the KV cached is not fully written back when the decoding is already finished, we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching. The unfinished KV caches are temporarily moved to the write buffer to avoid blocking the execution of the next job."
checks.section: §3.2.2 Asynchronous Saving from HBMs to Memory (Fig. 8)

checks.claim: Asynchronous saving reduces total execution time by 13-15%.
checks.correction: Correct. Missing context: the 13-15% is from one microbenchmark. Settings: LLaMA-13B on a single GPU, batch size 16, prompt lengths 1K to 1.6K, and 20 decoding steps. Only 20 decode steps leaves little decode time to hide the writes. Do not cite it as a general end-to-end number.
checks.quote: "Asynchronous KV cache saving. We set different prompt lengths ranging from 1K to 1.6K and the number of decoding steps to 20 for investigating the effectiveness of the asynchronous saving scheme. As Figure 20 shows, the saving time increases as the prompt length grows, as the size of the KV cache to be saved increases. To reduce the saving overhead, CachedAttention employs the asynchronous saving scheme allowing KV cache saving to overlap with inference execution, reducing the overall execution time by 13% to 15%."
checks.section: §4.3.2 Overlapped KV cache Access (Fig. 20)

checks.claim: The paper rejects LRU and FIFO because they rely solely on historical access information.
checks.correction: Substantively correct. The paper contrasts itself with LRU/FIFO for relying only on historical access information, and in the evaluation blames their low hit rates on lacking future-access information. Two nuances: (a) 'rejects' only means 'does not adopt'; LRU and FIFO are still used as evaluation baselines in §4.3.3. (b) The 'future access information' CachedAttention uses is only the scheduler's job queue of requests that have already arrived ('the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs', §3.3.1). It is a look-ahead window over queued jobs, not a prediction of when an idle session will return. The paper does not say how it picks among items outside the window. Verified identical in arXiv v3 (same file as the current arxiv.org/pdf/2403.19708), the USENIX ATC'24 PDF and arXiv v1 (titled AttentionStore).

(§3.3.2). The arXiv listing shows v1 23 Mar 2024, v2 16 Apr 2024 and v3 30 Jun 2024, with the comment 'Accepted to USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2024'. A larger buffer, sized S_buf = B(T_load*L_hist - T_pref*L_new), covers cases where loading takes longer than prefill. In the ablation, pre-loading without a buffer cuts prefill time by 35% and with a 15-layer buffer by 61% (Sec 4.3.2).

For comparison, LRU and FIFO get only about 0.6% and 0.5% DRAM hit rates at 128G/10T.

The second clause is not stated anywhere: it is an inference, but the paper's own design supports it. §4.3.3 is one combined experiment, CA (scheduler-aware fetching plus eviction) against 'existing eviction policies'. None of the ablations in §4.3.1 to §4.3.8 isolates fetching (for example LRU plus prefetch, or CA eviction without prefetch). The paper does credit the two mechanisms in prose without measuring them: it attributes the higher overall hit rate to eviction ('aware of the future KV cache access information to avoid evicting...') and the low baseline DRAM hit rates to the missing prefetch. Note also that the paper describes the baselines only as eviction policies ('existing eviction policies (including LRU and FIFO)'), even though they also lack prefetching.

checks.claim: CachedAttention appeared at USENIX ATC '24 (arXiv 2403.19708). v1 and v2 were titled 'AttentionStore'. In v3/ATC, AttentionStore names only the KV caching system (host DRAM + SSD).
checks.correction: Each part checks out. The arXiv abs page comment reads 'Accepted to USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2024'. The USENIX page lists it in '2024 USENIX Annual Technical Conference (USENIX ATC 24)'. v1 (23 Mar 2024) and v2 (16 Apr 2024) are titled 'AttentionStore: Cost-effective Attention Reuse across Multi-turn Conversations in Large Language Model Serving'. In those versions AttentionStore names the whole mechanism ('this paper proposes AttentionStore, a new attention mechanism'), and the caching system is just called 'the KV caching system'. In v3 (30 Jun 2024), which matches the ATC proceedings text, the mechanism is renamed CachedAttention and AttentionStore names only the KV caching system. Its tiers are given as 'host memory and disks'. The paper says 'disks', but the testbed uses SSDs. In Figure 5, the AttentionStore box contains host memory and disks, and the HBMs sit separately in the GPU cluster.

checks.claim: The paper does not model inter-turn think time.
checks.correction: Accurate, but only because the paper never mentions it, so state it carefully. The paper's only timing model is Poisson session arrivals: λ = 1.0 sessions/s end-to-end, and 0.5 to 2.0/s in §4.3.8. It never says when a session's follow-up turns arrive (no think-time distribution, gap or delay parameter). The wording 'does not specify or model' is safer than implying turns arrive back-to-back. The closest time-based mechanism is a per-session KV TTL, which is a retention limit and not a model of when the user returns: 'the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access', set to one hour in §4.3.6. Prefetching is driven by the job queue: §3.3.1 says 'the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs'. It is not driven by a predicted return time. I checked both arXiv v3 and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF. Neither contains 'think', 'interval', 'inter-turn' or a gap distribution.
checks.quote: "As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0). 9K conversation sessions are used in the experiments." (Also §4.3.6: "In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access. ... In the experiment, we set the TTL to one hour.")

checks.claim: The paper does not report queue depth or the lead time before execution.
checks.correction: Accurate, again because the paper never reports these numbers. The paper defines how long the windows are allowed to be: a prefetch window Lpw = Cmem/Skv and an eviction window (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv. It only shows example sizes in the Figure 9 illustration (prefetch window 2, eviction window 6). It never reports measured job-queue depth, the window lengths actually used in the experiments, or how far ahead of execution prefetches were issued or finished. It says only that prefetch happens 'before these waiting jobs are executed'. The closest reported result is outcome-only: over 99.6% of hits are DRAM hits (§4.3.3). '24 batches' in §4.1 is a batch setting, not a queue depth.
checks.quote: "Specifically, the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." (§4.3.3 result: "In contrast, CA achieves a cache hit rate of up to 86%, with over 99.6% of the hits occurring in DRAM due to its scheduler-aware policy.")

checks.correction: Mostly confirmed. 'Defined threshold' is a direct quote, and the paper gives no value for it. The paper never uses the terms write-through or write-back, so 'not by write-through' is an inference from that described save path, not an explicit statement. Two caveats: (a) §3.3.2 words the trigger differently, as free host memory being 'exhausted', not reaching a threshold; (b) in the Fig. 9 example, eviction is triggered to restore the host-memory buffer after a prefetch (Job 3) uses it. checks.correction: Confirmed. The words 'inclusive' and 'exclusive' do not appear anywhere in arXiv v3 or the ATC'24 PDF. The evidence for exclusive tiers is stronger than wording alone, because the Fig. 9 example needs a free disk slot to evict Job 4 from DRAM: Job 9 is evicted from disk and Job 4 moves into its slot. That would be unnecessary if Job 4's KV were already on disk (an inclusive design). Even so, this remains an inference. The paper does not say whether a KV prefetched from disk to DRAM (Job 3) is deleted from disk.
checks.quote: §3.3.2: "When the KV cache of Job 3 is chosen to be migrated to the host memory, the buffer will be utilized. ... Therefore, the KV cache for Job 4 is selected to be evicted from the host memory to the disks. Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted. Finally, the KV cache for Job 4 is moved to the location previously occupied by Job 9." §4.1: "Separate IO threads migrate data between the host memory and the disks, overlapping the execution with the KV cache migrations."
checks.section: §3.3.2 (Fig. 9 example); §4.1 Experimental Setup

checks.claim: 3. CA stores K and V before the positional encoding is applied, so saved KV can be truncated on context overflow. This requires relative positional encoding.
checks.correction: Confirmed. One minor point: under RPE the paper applies positional encoding to Q and K, not to V (Fig. 11b), so 'before positional encoding' only changes anything for K. When the KV is loaded, the paper re-applies new positional encodings.
checks.quote: §3.4: "CachedAttention needs to work with the relative position encoding (RPE) [42, 44, 54]. Unlike the absolute positional encoding (APE) in which positional encodings are added to the input, RPE directly embeds the positional encodings in the query (Q) and key (K) vectors ... By simply moving the time of caching KVs before embedding positional encodings in RPE as shown in Figure 11c, CachedAttention can store the KVs without embedded positional encodings in AttentionStore. When reusing the KVs in CachedAttention, the KVs are embedded with the new positional encodings". §1: "After decoupling, truncation can be directly applied to the KV caches, thereby ensuring the reusability of the saved KV caches."
checks.section: §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation; §1 Introduction; Fig. 11

checks.claim: 4. CA has no prefix tree and no cross-session prefix sharing.
checks.correction: The paper never says CA lacks these. The claim is inferred from what the paper leaves out. What it does state is that reuse is within 'the same session' and that the unit of caching, fetching and eviction is a whole session's KV. It describes no prefix tree or cross-session sharing for CA. Prefix sharing is mentioned only in Related Work, for RadixAttention and ChunkAttention as concurrent work. There the paper's stated difference from them is its use of slower, larger storage tiers, not the absence of prefix sharing. Safer wording: 'CA as described reuses KV only within a session, at whole-session granularity, and describes no prefix tree or cross-session sharing.'
checks.quote: §1: "We propose CachedAttention, a new attention that allows the reuse of the KV caches for any ensuing conversation turns of the same session". §3.3.2: "Note that one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session, which is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity in CachedAttention. This is because the KV cache in the same conversation session is either all used or none of it is used." §5: "RadixAttention and ChunkAttention optimize the inference tasks that share prompt prefixes. ... Different from all these works, CachedAttention exploits slower but larger storage hierarchies"
checks.section: §1 Introduction (contributions); §3.3.2; §5 Related Work

checks.claim: 5. CA's eviction ablation compares it with LRU and FIFO baselines that also lack prefetching, so the contributions of fetching and eviction are never measured separately. At 128G/10T the hit rates are CA 86%, LRU 58% and FIFO 48%.
checks.correction: Confirmed for arXiv v2, v3 and ATC'24. The paper says LRU and FIFO 'cannot pre-fetch'. No other experiment separates fetching from eviction: §4.3.7 varies storage tiers (HBM, HBM+DRAM, full CA), not policies. Version caveat: arXiv v1 (titled 'AttentionStore') reports different numbers at 128G/10T, AS 76%, LRU 31%, FIFO 48%. Cite v3 or ATC'24 for 86/58/48.
checks.quote: §4.3.3: "We evaluate the effectiveness of the scheduler-aware fetching and eviction in CachedAttention upon improving the cache hit rate. We compare overall cache hit rates, DRAM hit rates, and disk hit rates of CA and existing eviction policies (including LRU and FIFO) across various storage configurations. ... With the increased SSD capacity (128G/10T), CA achieves a remarkable hit rate of 86%, surpassing LRU (58%) and FIFO (48%). ... This is because LRU and FIFO lack awareness of future KV cache information and cannot pre-fetch KV caches from disks to host memory"
checks.section: §4.3.3 Scheduler-aware Fetching and Eviction; Fig. 21 ('Comparison of the eviction algorithms under various storage settings')

checks.claim: 6. In that ablation, over 99.6% of CA's hits are DRAM hits.
checks.correction: Verbatim in v2, v3 and ATC'24. arXiv v1 says 'over 99.9%'. The sentence pairs the figure with 'up to 86%', so it clearly covers the 128G/10T configuration, but the paper gives no breakdown per configuration. The paper also does not define whether a KV prefetched from SSD before its job runs counts as a DRAM hit. The 'due to its scheduler-aware policy' wording suggests it does, but that is an inference.
checks.quote: §4.3.3: "In contrast, CA achieves a cache hit rate of up to 86%, with over 99.6% of the hits occurring in DRAM due to its scheduler-aware policy."
checks.section: §4.3.3 Scheduler-aware Fetching and Eviction

checks.claim: In CA's Fig. 9 example, the KV of a queued job outside the window (Job 9, 'the last arrived') is dropped out of the system.
checks.correction: Supported. In the rendered Figure 9, the 'eviction window, size: 6' bracket spans Job 2 through Job 7. Job 8 and Job 9 are queued but outside it, and an arrow leads from KV 9 down out of the 'disks' box. The text says Job 9 is 'the most suitable candidate to be evicted' and does not use the word 'dropped'. That it leaves the system follows from the opening of §3.3.2: when the disks are full, KV is evicted 'out of the system'. The text never says Job 9 is outside the window; only the figure shows that. It also gives no rule for choosing Job 9 over Job 8 (also outside the window) other than calling Job 9 'last arrived'. The USENIX ATC'24 PDF has the same text.
checks.quote: "Meanwhile, if the disks are full, we also need to evict some KV caches stored in the disks out of the system." ... "Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted. Finally, the KV cache for Job 4 is moved to the location previously occupied by Job 9."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks (Figure 9 example); Figure 9 (page 7, arXiv v3)

checks.claim: CA explicitly rejects LRU and FIFO because they 'solely rely on the historical access information of the KV caches'.
checks.correction: The quoted phrase is verbatim. One wording point: the paper sets its scheme against LRU/FIFO with 'Different from...' and does not use the word 'reject'. It does pick its own scheduler-aware scheme for that stated reason. In §4.3.3 it compares against LRU and FIFO and says they 'lack awareness of future KV cache information'.
checks.quote: "Different from the existing cache eviction strategies, such as the least-recently-used (LRU) [46], first-in-first-out (FIFO) [8], and their variants, which solely rely on the historical access information of the KV caches, CachedAttention presents a scheduler-aware eviction scheme which can leverage the future access information of KV caches to achieve a higher cache hit rate." (§4.3.3: "This is because LRU and FIFO lack awareness of future KV cache information and cannot pre-fetch KV caches from disks to host memory")
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; §4.3.3 Scheduler-aware Fetching and Eviction

checks.claim: CA's minimal eviction and fetching unit is one whole session's KV, justified because a session's KV 'is either all used or none of it is used'.
checks.quote: "Note that one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session, which is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity in CachedAttention. This is because the KV cache in the same conversation session is either all used or none of it is used."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks

checks.claim: CA makes no prediction of when a session's next turn will arrive. Nothing is fetched or protected for a session with no queued job, and the eviction order among such sessions is not specified.
checks.correction: Consistent with the paper, which never mentions predicting when the next turn arrives. Its only 'future access information' is the scheduler's job queue, and it treats requests as arriving randomly. Prefetching covers only waiting jobs inside the prefetching window, and exemption from eviction covers only items inside the eviction window. One nuance: the Fig. 9 example first checks whether every host-memory KV has a queued job. That implies KV with no queued job would be evicted before anything in the window, but the paper gives no order among such KV.
checks.quote: "As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks" (§3.3.1); "the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs" (§3.3.1); "if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted" (§3.3.2); "First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue. It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head" (§3.3.2 example)
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks

checks.claim: CA's only rule for idle sessions is a TTL measured from last access (1 hour in §4.3.6). It appears only in the capacity-sizing analysis, and its interaction with the eviction windows is not specified.
checks.correction: These parts are accurate: the TTL is measured since last access, it is set to one hour in the §4.3.6 experiment, the term appears only in §4.3.6 (in both the arXiv v3 and ATC'24 PDFs), and the paper never says how it interacts with the prefetch or eviction windows. 'Only rule for idle sessions' goes too far. §3.1 also says an inactive session's KV is saved to AttentionStore instead of being discarded. Idle sessions' KV is also subject to the scheduler-aware eviction: it gets no window exemption, and the Fig. 9 example checks host-memory KV for an associated queued job first. Also, the paper describes the TTL as a property of CachedAttention itself ('In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL'), not only as an assumption for the analysis, although it is introduced only inside the capacity-sizing subsection.
checks.quote: "In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access. The TTL is set as the unit time mentioned above." ... "In the experiment, we set the TTL to one hour." (§4.3.6); "when the associated conversation session is inactive, CachedAttention saves the KV cache in a KV caching system, named AttentionStore, instead of discarding them" (§3.1)
checks.section: §4.3.6 The Cache Capacity Requirement; §3.1 Overview

checks.claim: CA does not model inter-turn think time. Its evaluation uses ShareGPT with Poisson session arrivals (λ = 1.0, swept from 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s).
checks.correction: These parts are verbatim-supported: ShareGPT, Poisson session arrivals with λ = 1.0, and the 0.5/s to 2.0/s sweep (§4.3.8, run on LLaMA-13B with 128GB/10TB; the Fig. 25 axis ticks go to 2.5, but the text says 0.5 to 2.0). 'Does not model inter-turn think time' is not stated; the paper is silent. It says request arrival times come from a Poisson distribution and that session arrivals per second are Poisson, but it never says how a session's later turns are timed. It does not say turns run back to back or after a think-time gap. The claim should read: 'the paper does not describe any inter-turn timing or think-time model'.
checks.quote: "As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0). 9K conversation sessions are used in the experiments." (§4.1); "In the experiments, we configure the session arrival rates varying from 0.5/s to 2.0/s. We test LLaMA-13B with 128GB/10TB storage following warmup as before." (§4.3.8)
checks.section: §4.1 Experimental Setup (Workloads); §4.3.8 Impact of Session Arrival Rates

checks.claim: CachedAttention (USENIX ATC '24; arXiv 2403.19708 v3) saves the KV caches of all requests in AttentionStore, a KV caching system made of host DRAM and SSDs, and reuses them for later turns of the same session.
checks.correction: No correction needed. Bibliographic check: arXiv v3 (30 Jun 2024) is the latest version and carries the comment "Accepted to USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2024". USENIX lists it in ATC '24, pp. 111-126. One caveat: "save for all requests" describes what gets written, not how long it stays. Entries can be evicted "out of the system" when disks are full (§3.3.2), and each session's KV has a TTL (§4.3.6), so later reuse depends on a cache hit (86/71/89/90% in §4.2). It is not guaranteed.
checks.quote: Abstract: "CachedAttention maintains a hierarchical KV caching system that leverages cost-effective memory/storage mediums to save KV caches for all requests." §1: "When a conversation session becomes inactive, CachedAttention saves the corresponding KV cache in a KV caching system, named AttentionStore. Upon the resumption of the same session, CachedAttention loads and reuses the saved KV cache from AttentionStore". §3.1: "CachedAttention employs multi-tier cost-effective storage mediums in AttentionStore, i.e., host memory and disks." §3.3: "The access speed of host memory, i.e., DRAM, is much higher than disks, i.e., SSDs, (tens of GB/s v.s. several GB/s)." §4.3.6: "the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access."
checks.section: Abstract; §1 Introduction; §3.1 Overview (Figure 5); §3.3; §3.3.2; §4.3.6

checks.claim: In CachedAttention, HBM holds the execution buffer plus reserved read and write buffers and is not used as a cross-turn KV cache tier.
checks.correction: Substantively correct, with three notes. (1) The paper never says in so many words that HBM is not a cache tier. The point is shown by Figure 5, where the AttentionStore box contains only Host memory and Disks and GPU0/HBM0 and GPU1/HBM1 sit outside it in the GPU Cluster, and by the §2.4 and §4.3.7 wording below. (2) The three buffers are not everything in HBM: §2.4 notes that "130 GB of HBM space is allocated to store the model", and running jobs' KV is in HBM during execution. (3) §4.3.7 has one ambiguous phrase. After an HBM+DRAM baseline it says "by further extending the cache capacity with SSDs, CachedAttention improves the cache hit rate", which could be read as that experiment's CA config keeping the 10GB HBM cache. However, the same section's framing sentence and the whole design section put CA's cache on DRAM and SSDs.
checks.quote: §3.2.1: "when the GPU starts computing the self-attention for a layer, the corresponding KV cache of the layer is already in the HBM execution buffer." ... "CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap." §3.2.2: "we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching. The unfinished KV caches are temporarily moved to the write buffer to avoid blocking the execution of the next job." §2.4: "the KV caches of historical conversations can be saved in a KV caching system out of GPUs." §4.3.7: "Some existing works [18,28,63] employ only the HBM space for caching the KV caches of multi-turn conversations. We here compare the performance of mechanism caching KVs on HBMs with that of CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs."

checks.claim: CachedAttention does not predict when a session's next turn will arrive or be admitted.
checks.correction: Correct as a negative claim. I searched the full v3 text for predict, forecast, estimat, arriv, interval, idle, inactive and TTL. Nothing predicts a session's next-turn arrival or admission time. The paper treats arrivals as random, and its evaluation draws arrivals from a Poisson distribution. Nuance: its "future access information" is the order of jobs already in the scheduler's waiting queue. It therefore knows the relative order of admissions that are about to happen for requests that have already arrived, but nothing about turns that have not arrived yet, and it never estimates a time. Cache retention beyond the queue is handled by eviction plus a fixed TTL since last access, not by any timing prediction.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks, resulting in poor access performance." ... "the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed." §3.3.2: "CachedAttention presents a scheduler-aware eviction scheme which can leverage the future access information of KV caches to achieve a higher cache hit rate. The job queue in the job scheduler gives us the opportunity to achieve this." §4.1: "we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates"

checks.claim: CachedAttention's scheduler-aware fetching prefetches disk-resident KV into host memory for waiting jobs inside a head-anchored look-ahead prefetching window over the scheduler's job queue.
checks.correction: No correction needed. "Head-anchored" is not in the text. It comes from Figure 9, where the job queue is labeled "head" at the Job 2 end. The "prefetching window, size: 2" bracket covers Job 3 and Job 2, the jobs next in line while Job 1 runs. The "eviction window, size: 6" bracket covers Job 7 through Job 2 and is also anchored at the head.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "we leverage a scheduler-aware KV cache fetching scheme to pre-fetch the KV caches to be accessed from disks to the host memory. This is done by utilizing the hints from the inference job scheduler. ... CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed." ... "As Job 1 is executing, the KV cache manager applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; Figure 9

checks.claim: The prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs, where Cmem is the host memory available for prefetching and Skv is the average per-session KV size.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The unit ("jobs") is not written next to the formula. It follows from the Figure 9 example, where 2 host-memory KV slots give a window covering waiting Jobs 2-3. One item is one session's KV (§3.3.2), so dividing by the per-session size gives a count of jobs/sessions.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv."

checks.claim: The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs, described as a maximum set by the total capacity of AttentionStore.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The word "maximum" appears in the sentence before the formula. The formula sentence itself just says "The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv". Cmem is the term defined in §3.3.1 as "available memory capacity for prefetching", and Cdisk is "the total available capacity in the disks". In the Figure 9 example the eviction window is size 6. That equals the 2 DRAM "cache use" slots plus 4 disk slots and leaves out the DRAM "sys use" region (KV 1 + buf), which suggests capacities are counted net of system-reserved memory.
checks.quote: §3.3.2: "Specifically, CachedAttention maintains a look-ahead eviction window in the job queue. The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv. When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: 1. CA saves KV caches for all requests in a host DRAM + SSD hierarchy (AttentionStore) instead of discarding them. It fetches them back when the same session is activated again.
checks.correction: The statement is right. Two caveats: (a) 'saved' does not mean kept forever. When the disks are full, items are evicted out of AttentionStore (§3.3.2), and in §4.3.6 each session's KV has a TTL ('maximum saving time since the last access'; set to one hour in the experiment). (b) Saving is per session and happens when the session goes inactive. The KV is written asynchronously, layer by layer, during prefill and decode (§3.2.2). The wording is the same in the ATC'24 version and arXiv v3; v1 called the whole system 'AttentionStore'.
checks.quote: Abstract: "CachedAttention maintains a hierarchical KV caching system that leverages cost-effective memory/storage mediums to save KV caches for all requests." §3.1: "when the associated conversation session is inactive, CachedAttention saves the KV cache in a KV caching system, named AttentionStore, instead of discarding them as in the conventional attention mechanism. If the same conversation session is activated in the future, its KV cache is fetched from AttentionStore and reused for inference." §3.1: "CachedAttention employs multi-tier cost-effective storage mediums in AttentionStore, i.e., host memory and disks." §3.3: "The access speed of host memory, i.e., DRAM, is much higher than disks, i.e., SSDs, (tens of GB/s v.s. several GB/s)."
checks.section: Abstract; §1 Introduction; §3.1 Overview; §3.3 Hierarchical KV Cache Placement (ATC'24 version = arXiv v3)

checks.claim: 2. In CA, HBM is not a cross-turn cache tier. It holds the execution buffer plus reserved read and write buffers, and HBM-only retention (LMDeploy, RadixAttention) is treated as prior work or a baseline.
checks.correction: The substance is right, but the paper never says in so many words that HBM is not a cache tier. That follows from three things: AttentionStore is defined as host memory plus disks, §3.2.2 says cross-turn reuse comes from saving to host memory, and §4.3.7 contrasts 'caching KVs on HBMs' with 'CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs'. On baselines: the main evaluation baseline is RE (recomputation). HBM-only and HBM+DRAM appear only as comparison configurations in §4.3.7 (10GB HBM cache, cites [18,28,63], i.e. LMDeploy, FasterTransformer, SGLang). In §5, RadixAttention is called work 'developed concurrently' and is described as prefix sharing. The intro, however, groups [18,63] as 'prior works' that keep KV in HBM.
checks.quote: §1: "Prior works have attempted to reduce the inefficiency of repetitive KV computation by retaining the KV caches across multi-turn conversations in HBMs [18,63]. However, this quickly exhausts the limited HBM capacity." §3.2.1: "the corresponding KV cache of the layer is already in the HBM execution buffer" ... "CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap." §3.2.2: "CachedAttention needs to save KV caches to host memory to enable the reuse of the KV caches across conversations." ... "we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching." §4.3.7: "Some existing works [18,28,63] employ only the HBM space for caching the KV caches of multi-turn conversations. We here compare the performance of mechanism caching KVs on HBMs with that of CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs." §4.1: "Baseline. We compare CachedAttention (CA) with re-computation (RE)." §5: "LMDeploy [18] is an LLM inference framework that caches the KV caches of multi-turn conversations on HBMs. RadixAttention [63], ChunkAttention [56], and Pensieve [58] are inference techniques that were developed concurrently with CachedAttention."
checks.section: §1 Introduction; §3.2.1; §3.2.2; §4.1 Baseline; §4.3.7 Impact of Caching Storage Mediums; §5 Related Work

checks.claim: 3. CA's disk->DRAM prefetch applies only to waiting jobs in the scheduler's job queue. They must lie within a head-anchored look-ahead prefetching window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs.
checks.correction: Right in substance, with three caveats. (a) 'Head-anchored' comes from Figure 9 and its worked example, not the main text. The figure draws the prefetching window (size 2) over Jobs 2-3, next to the 'head' label, while Job 1 runs. The prose never uses the word 'head' for this window. (b) Cmem here is 'the available memory capacity for prefetching', not total DRAM. In Fig. 9 it is the 2 DRAM 'cache use' slots ('the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching'). (c) The paper never literally says 'only'. But the one prefetch trigger it describes is a waiting job inside the window whose KV is on disk. Nothing prefetches for sessions whose next turn has not yet arrived.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." Example: "As Job 1 is executing, the KV cache manager applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3." Figure 9 labels: "prefetching window, size: 2", "head".
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; Figure 9

checks.claim: 4. CA's windows are counted in jobs and sized by capacity, using the average per-session KV size Skv. They contain no time, disk-bandwidth or read-backlog term.
checks.correction: Right. Both window formulas are pure capacity divided by Skv, laid over the job queue, with no time, bandwidth or backlog term. Two clarifications: the eviction window length is described as a 'maximum length'. And the paper does use a bandwidth-based sizing formula elsewhere, but only for the HBM pre-loading read buffer (§3.2.1, Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew), where B is PCIe bandwidth). That formula is not used for the disk/DRAM windows.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." §3.3.2: "The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem +Cdisk)/Skv." (Contrast, §3.2.1: "Combined with the PCIe bandwidth B, the buffer size can be set by the following formula: Sbuf = B(TloadLhist −Tpref Lnew).")
checks.section: §3.3.1; §3.3.2; (§3.2.1 for the only bandwidth-based sizing, which is for the HBM read buffer)

checks.claim: 5. CA's look-ahead eviction window is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs long. An item whose job is inside it is exempt from eviction out of AttentionStore.
checks.correction: Right. One wording point: the paper gives (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv as the window's 'maximum length', set by AttentionStore's total capacity. In Fig. 9 the window is 6 jobs (Jobs 2-7), which equals 2 DRAM cache slots plus 4 disk slots. Job 9, the most recent arrival, is outside the window and is the one evicted out of the disk tier. The exemption applies to eviction out of AttentionStore. DRAM->disk demotion uses tail priority instead (see statement 6).
checks.quote: §3.3.2: "Specifically, CachedAttention maintains a look-ahead eviction window in the job queue. The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem +Cdisk)/Skv. When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted." Example: "Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: 6. For DRAM->disk demotion, CA evicts the item nearest the tail of the look-ahead eviction window first, scanning from tail to head.
checks.correction: The tail-first rule is stated, but the statement leaves out a step and makes the rule sound stricter than the paper does. (a) In the worked example, CA first checks whether every DRAM-resident KV has an associated job in the job queue. Only because they all do does it 'then' scan tail to head. This implies that a DRAM item with no queued job (or one outside the window) would be the first victim; the paper does not spell out that case. (b) The general rule is phrased as priority: the item at the tail 'has a higher priority to be evicted'. It is not stated as a strict ordering. Also, one item is a whole session's KV, which is the minimum granularity for both eviction and fetching.
checks.quote: §3.3.2: "When CachedAttention evicts one item from the host memory to disks, the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted. Note that one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session, which is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity in CachedAttention." Example: "CachedAttention employs a look-ahead eviction window of size 6 to monitor the KV cache status of the jobs. First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue. It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail. Therefore, the KV cache for Job 4 is selected to be evicted from the host memory to the disks."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: The paper does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk or being fetched.
checks.correction: Confirmed silent in arXiv v1, v2 and v3 and in the USENIX ATC'24 PDF. The fetch rule only says the prefetch happens 'before these waiting jobs are executed'. No text covers a fetch that is late or still running when the job is dispatched: no stall, no direct disk-to-HBM path, no recompute fallback. The paper does give two indirect hints. KV that is on disk at access time causes 'poor inference performance'. Disk hits also count as hits in the hit-rate figures (Fig. 13, Fig. 21; CA has 'over 99.6% of the hits occurring in DRAM', so about 0.4% are disk hits). That means disk-resident KV is still reused on some path. However, §3.2.1 describes loading into HBM only 'from the host memory', and the disk-hit path is never described.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed." §2.4 (Challenge 3): "As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks when being accessed, resulting in poor inference performance." §4.3.3: "CA achieves a cache hit rate of up to 86%, with over 99.6% of the hits occurring in DRAM due to its scheduler-aware policy."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; §2.4; §3.2.1; §4.2 (Fig. 13); §4.3.3

checks.claim: Because CachedAttention fetches only for jobs already in the queue, a fetch's lead time is bounded by the job's queueing delay (an inference from the fetch rule, not stated in the paper).
checks.correction: The statement is labeled correctly as an inference: the paper never states a lead-time bound. The premise holds. The only prefetch trigger the paper describes is a look-ahead window over waiting jobs in the scheduler's queue, and there is no prediction of future turns before the request arrives. The paper does not literally say 'only'. The bound is actually tighter than queueing delay. A fetch can start only once the job is within the first Lpw = Cmem/Skv waiting positions, not when it enters the queue. So lead time is at most the time the job spends inside the prefetch window, and that is no more than its queueing delay.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "Specifically, the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory (and Fig. 9)

checks.claim: The paper treats conversation requests as arriving randomly.
checks.correction: Stated verbatim three times (§1, §2.4, §3.3.1) and used as the reason that most KV caches are on disk when accessed. In the evaluation, arrivals are modeled with a Poisson process: 'sessions arriving per second', λ = 1.0, and §4.3.8 varies the session rate from 0.5/s to 2.0/s. The paper does not say how the timing of later turns within a session (the inter-turn gap) is generated. It notes that ShareGPT has no timestamps.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks, resulting in poor access performance." §4.1: "As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0)."
checks.section: §1 Introduction; §2.4 (Challenge 3); §3.3.1; §4.1 Experimental Setup (Workloads)

checks.claim: CachedAttention takes the scheduler as given and only reads its job queue; execution from the queue head in arrival order is implied, though FCFS is never named.
checks.correction: No version contains 'FCFS', 'first-come' or 'arrival order'. 'FIFO' appears only as a baseline eviction policy. The paper proposes no scheduling policy and only 'leverages the hints' from the scheduler's job queue. Execution from the head in arrival order is implied in three ways: Fig. 9 labels the queue 'head', next to the executing Job 1; the prefetch window covers the next waiting jobs (Jobs 2-3); and the tail is 'the last arrived Job 9'. Two minor caveats. First, Fig. 5 draws the 'Job Queue' and 'Job Scheduler' inside the 'CachedAttention Controller' box, but nothing about them is designed. Second, §4.1 says 'Continuous batching [57] is enabled through experiments', so jobs from the head join a running batch rather than running one at a time.
checks.quote: §3.1: "we present a scheduler-aware fetching scheme that leverages the hints from the job scheduler to prefetch KV caches to be accessed from disks to host memory." §3.3.1: "the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs." §3.3.2: "It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail... Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted."

checks.claim: CachedAttention stores K and V before the positional encoding is applied and re-applies new positions at load time, so saved KV can be truncated on context overflow.
checks.correction: One detail is more precise in the paper. Under RPE the positional encoding is embedded only in Q and K (Fig. 11b), and Fig. 12 marks the re-applied position as 'Position (on key)'. V carries no positional encoding, so new positions are re-applied to the keys. The paper loosely calls this re-embedding into 'the KV caches'. Truncation happens on the saved KV (Fig. 12: pos [0:2048] to pos [0:1536]) before it is loaded into HBM, and new encodings are applied afterwards.
checks.quote: §3.4: "By simply moving the time of caching KVs before embedding positional encodings in RPE as shown in Figure 11c, CachedAttention can store the KVs without embedded positional encodings in AttentionStore. When reusing the KVs in CachedAttention, the KVs are embedded with the new positional encodings and further used for the following inference." §1: "CachedAttention decouples the positional encoding from the KV caches when saving them. It re-embeds the positional encoding into KV caches when loading them. After decoupling, truncation can be directly applied to the KV caches, thereby ensuring the reusability of the saved KV caches."
checks.section: §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation (Figs. 11-12); §1; §3.1

checks.claim: Positional-encoding-decoupled truncation requires relative positional encoding.
checks.correction: Stated directly. The paper contrasts RPE with absolute positional encoding (APE), where encodings are added to the input, so APE models are not covered. Its 'RPE' category is the kind applied to Q and K, and it lists LLaMA, T5, Falcon, Mistral, Mixtral and Transformer-XL as examples.
checks.quote: §3.4: "To address this problem, CachedAttention enables the KV caches after truncation to be still valid via decoupling the positional encoding. CachedAttention needs to work with the relative position encoding (RPE) [42, 44, 54]. Unlike the absolute positional encoding (APE) in which positional encodings are added to the input, RPE directly embeds the positional encodings in the query (Q) and key (K) vectors, as shown in Figure 11b."
checks.section: §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation

checks.claim: In the evaluation, the truncation ratio is 0.5 (the earliest half of the tokens is discarded on overflow).
checks.correction: No correction needed. One scope note: the 0.5 sentence sits in the Baseline paragraph and is written about RE (recomputation). For CA, the paper does not restate the ratio in the evaluation setup. The same ratio is implied by §3.4 and the Figure 10 caption ('Context window size: 4K, truncation ratio: 2K'), which show both the baseline and CA cutting the first 2K of a 4K window. The Figure 12 example (pos [0:2048] -> KV [0:1536]) is only an illustration and is not the evaluated ratio. The sentence is the same in arXiv v1, v2 and v3 and in the USENIX ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "When the historical tokens exceed the context window limitation, RE applies token truncation, same as the general LLM services [30]. For simplicity, the token truncation ratio is set to 0.5, implying that when an overflow occurs, the system will discard the earliest half of the tokens." (§4.1) Also §3.4: "As shown in Figure 10a, the context window size is 4K. Once the context window overflows, the LLM serving engines cut off the first 2K tokens of the prompt."
checks.section: §4.1 Experimental Setup (Baseline paragraph); §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation / Figure 10 caption

checks.claim: Perplexity with CachedAttention's truncation is within 0.02 of recompute-based token truncation.
checks.correction: No correction needed. Two notes: (a) The text says the difference is '< 0.02', but its own Table 1 has one gap of exactly 0.02 (C4, LLaMA-7B: CA 6.96 vs TT 6.98). All other gaps are 0.01. So 'within 0.02' (at most 0.02) matches the table, and the paper's strict '<' is off by one case. CA is sometimes slightly better than TT and sometimes slightly worse. (b) Scope: PPL was measured only on LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-13B with WikiText-2, PTB and C4. These are not the end-to-end models (13B/65B/70B/Falcon-40B). Naive KV truncation (NKVT) gives PPL above 1000. TT is defined as removing historical tokens and recomputing the KV for the remaining tokens, so 'recompute-based token truncation' is a fair description.
checks.quote: "TT consistently achieves a low PPL by recomputing KV caches after context window overflow. CA also maintains a low PPL, comparable to TT (with a difference of< 0.02), by incorporating new positional encodings into the KV caches after truncation." Table 1 (CA / TT / NKVT): WikiText-2 LLaMA-7B 5.47/5.48/2198.7; LLaMA-13B 4.91/4.90/1647.7; PTB LLaMA-7B 8.48/8.49/2543.5; LLaMA-13B 7.61/7.60/1865.8; C4 LLaMA-7B 6.96/6.98/2343.5; LLaMA-13B 6.44/6.45/1745.6.
checks.section: §4.3.5 Accuracy of Decoupled Positional Encoding, Table 1

checks.claim: Compared with the OF baseline (positions embedded, so overflow invalidates the cache), CachedAttention's hit rates are higher by 17.6 / 41.5 / 18.1 / 18.4 points for LLaMA-13B / 65B / 70B / Falcon-40B.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The text writes the numbers as '%' and frames them as OF's hit rates decreasing compared with CA, which leaves open whether they are relative or absolute. I measured the bars in Figure 22a by pixel height (rendered at 400 dpi). CA is about 86 / 71.5 / 88.5 / 90.5 and OF is about 68 / 30 / 70.5 / 72, which gives gaps of about 17.5 / 41.7 / 17.9 / 18.0. That confirms absolute percentage points. A relative reading would put OF for 65B near 41.5%, and the bar shows about 30%. Setup: 128GB DRAM plus 10TB SSD. The large 65B gap comes from LLaMA-1-65B's 2K context window. Version caveat: arXiv v1 reported different numbers ('hit rates decrease by 52%, 56%, 57%, 48%'). The 17.6/41.5/18.1/18.4 figures are in v2, v3 and the ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "we compare a baseline approach overflow (OF) that embeds positional encoding within the KV caches, leading to the invalidation of KV caches in AttentionStore. OF relegates context overflow to be managed by recomputation. This experiment uses 128GB DRAM and 10TB SSD. As evident from Figure 22a, comparing OF with CA, the hit rates decrease by 17.6%, 41.5%, 18.1%, 18.4% for LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-65B, LLaMA-70B, and Falcon-40B, respectively." ... "OF of LLaMA-65B experiences a low hit rate due to its limited 2K context window."
checks.section: §4.3.4 Performance of Decoupled KV Cache Truncation, Figure 22a

checks.claim: CachedAttention describes compatibility with token-discarding lists (TDL) from KV-compression methods but does not evaluate it.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The paper calls it a 'token discarding list (TDL)'. TDL appears only in §3.4. The evaluation never mentions TDL or KV compression: §4.3.4 compares OF and CA, and §4.3.5 compares CA, TT and NKVT only. 'Compression' otherwise appears only in Related Work, which calls those techniques 'orthogonal', and in the references. Version note: the TDL paragraph is in arXiv v3 and the ATC'24 PDF but not in v1 or v2 (then titled 'AttentionStore').
checks.quote: "Note that CachedAttention also allows for selective preservation of certain KV cache for compression, e.g., the initial tokens with important scores [54] or important tokens [12,24,61], to further improve the generation quality of LLMs. Specifically, a given KV cache compression technique essentially provides a methodology for creating a token discarding list (TDL), in the prompt, e.g., discarding the least important tokens. CachedAttention straightforwardly complies with the TDL, discarding the KV cache associated with the TDL within the AttentionStore. After discarding the selected KV caches, AttentionStore delivers the pruned KV cache to the inference engine upon an inference execution."
checks.section: §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation (no matching evaluation in §4)

checks.claim: The evaluation uses ShareGPT with 9K sessions averaging 5.75 turns (about 52K turns): the first 10K turns warm up AttentionStore and the following 42K are evaluated.
checks.correction: No correction needed. This is stated for the end-to-end experiments in §4.2, and §4.1 also says 9K sessions are used. Version caveat: arXiv v1 gave an average of 3.51 turns, about 32K turns in total and 22K evaluated after a 10K warm-up. The 5.75 / 52K / 42K figures are in v2, v3 and the ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "In the end-to-end experiments, we use 9K conversations from ShareGPT [33] and the average number of turns in these conversations is 5.75. Thus the total number of conversation turns is about 52K. We warm up AttentionStore using the first 10K conversation turns and then evaluate the performance on the following 42K turns."
checks.section: §4.2 End-to-end Performance (also §4.1 Workloads: "9K conversation sessions are used in the experiments.")

checks.claim: Session arrivals are generated from a Poisson distribution with λ = 1.0 sessions/s, and §4.3.8 sweeps 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The unit 'sessions/s' comes from the wording 'number of different sessions arriving per second'. The §4.3.8 sweep covers only LLaMA-13B with 128GB/10TB, and hit rate falls from 82% to 77% as the rate rises from 0.5 to 2.0. Relevant to the comparison with your design: the paper does not say how later turns within a session are timed. It gives no inter-turn or think-time model and no per-session gap distribution, only the session-level Poisson rate. Its fetching and eviction rely on look-ahead windows over the scheduler's job queue, not on predicting when a session's next turn will arrive. Version note: the §4.3.8 arrival-rate study exists only in v3 and the ATC'24 PDF. In v1 and v2, §4.3.8 covers other topics.
checks.quote: "As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0). 9K conversation sessions are used in the experiments." (§4.1) and "In the experiments, we configure the session arrival rates varying from 0.5/s to 2.0/s. We test LLaMA-13B with 128GB/10TB storage following warmup as before." (§4.3.8)
checks.section: §4.1 Experimental Setup (Workloads); §4.3.8 Impact of Session Arrival Rates

checks.claim: CachedAttention describes a token-discarding-list (TDL) hook for KV compression methods, but does not evaluate it.
checks.correction: This holds. The only nuance is the word 'hook', which is ours, not the paper's. The paper says an external KV-compression technique 'provides' a TDL and that CachedAttention 'straightforwardly complies' with it by dropping the matching KV entries in AttentionStore before handing the pruned cache to the engine. The paper never says how this connects to the compression method in practice. No evaluation subsection (4.2, 4.3.1-4.3.8) tests TDL-based or importance-based compression. Sections 4.3.4 and 4.3.5 evaluate only contiguous prefix truncation when the context window overflows (decoupled positional encoding vs. OF/TT/NKVT). The only other mention of compression is Related Work, which calls quantization and compression techniques 'orthogonal to CachedAttention'. Checked against arXiv v3 (last revised 30 Jun 2024) and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF; the TDL text is the same in both.
checks.quote: "Note that CachedAttention also allows for selective preservation of certain KV cache for compression, e.g., the initial tokens with important scores [54] or important tokens [12,24,61], to further improve the generation quality of LLMs. Specifically, a given KV cache compression technique essentially provides a methodology for creating a token discarding list (TDL), in the prompt, e.g., discarding the least important tokens. CachedAttention straightforwardly complies with the TDL, discarding the KV cache associated with the TDL within the AttentionStore. After discarding the selected KV caches, AttentionStore delivers the pruned KV cache to the inference engine upon an inference execution." (Sec. 3.4). Evaluation covers only truncation: "We evaluate the impact of the different schemes including CA, token truncation (TT), and naive KV cache truncation (NKVT) on the perplexity (PPL) and the accuracy of LLMs" (Sec. 4.3.5). Related Work: "existing work employs quantization and compression techniques on KV caches [12, 24, 54, 61]... These techniques are orthogonal to CachedAttention" (Sec. 5).
checks.section: 3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation (TDL description); 4.3.4-4.3.5 (only truncation evaluated); 5 Related Work

checks.claim: CachedAttention generates session arrivals with a Poisson process (λ = 1.0 sessions/s by default, swept from 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s) on ShareGPT conversations, because the dataset has no arrival timestamps.
checks.correction: Every part is stated in the paper: the ShareGPT source, the missing timestamps as the reason, Poisson arrivals, λ = 1.0 sessions/s, and the 0.5-2.0/s sweep. Three qualifications. (1) The sweep (Sec. 4.3.8) uses only LLaMA-13B with 128GB DRAM / 10TB SSD; the other models run only at λ = 1.0. (2) The Figure 25 x-axis ticks go up to 2.5, but the text says the sweep is 0.5/s to 2.0/s. (3) The paper gives Poisson arrivals only for sessions. It never says how the later turns of a session are timed (no think-time, inter-turn gap or reply-delay model), so the gap between a session's turns in their workload is unknown. That matters when comparing against a design that predicts each session's next admission time. Other details: 9K ShareGPT sessions, 5.75 turns on average, about 52K turns, the first 10K turns used for warmup, and the Poisson method described as 'following prior works [21,52]'. Same text in arXiv v3 and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "Workloads. The workload is integrated from the ShareGPT dataset [33, 62]. As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0). 9K conversation sessions are used in the experiments." (Sec. 4.1). "In the experiments, we configure the session arrival rates varying from 0.5/s to 2.0/s. We test LLaMA-13B with 128GB/10TB storage following warmup as before." (Sec. 4.3.8)
checks.section: 4.1 Experimental Setup (Workloads); 4.3.8 Impact of Session Arrival Rates (Figure 25)

checks.claim: 1. Both windows are counted in jobs, sized by capacity, and take no account of time, disk bandwidth or read backlog.
checks.correction: Supported, with three caveats. (a) Both windows sit on the job queue. Their lengths are capacity divided by the average KV size of one session (Skv), so a window is a number of job slots estimated from that average, not an exact count of bytes. (b) The paper calls (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv the *maximum* length of the eviction window. (c) The 'no time, bandwidth or backlog' part is true because nothing is there: neither formula has such a term, and the paper never discusses one for the windows. Disk bandwidth appears only in the §2 motivation ('the disks have an access bandwidth of less than 5 GB/s'). PCIe bandwidth B appears only in the §3.2.1 HBM read-buffer size, Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew), which is unrelated to the prefetch and eviction windows. The wording is the same in arXiv v3 and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." ... "The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem +Cdisk)/Skv."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks

checks.claim: 2. Nothing is prefetched for a session that has no job in the queue.
checks.correction: The paper implies this but never says it outright. The only prefetch trigger it describes is a waiting job inside the look-ahead prefetching window, and no other disk-to-DRAM prefetch path exists. The real rule is narrower than the claim: only jobs in the first Lpw = Cmem/Skv queue positions are prefetched. In Fig. 9 only Jobs 2–3 are checked and only KV 3 is fetched. The intro says the scheme 'pre-fetches the KV caches that are likely to be accessed... by utilizing the hints received from the inference job scheduler'. There is no prediction for sessions without a queued job.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory (also Fig. 9 walkthrough)

checks.claim: 3. An item whose job is inside the look-ahead eviction window is exempt from being evicted out of AttentionStore.
checks.correction: Matches the text, with one scope note. The exemption covers only eviction *out of AttentionStore* (dropping from disk). It does not cover host-to-disk demotion, which can still pick items inside the window, as Job 4 shows in Fig. 9. One item is all the KV of one conversation session.
checks.quote: "When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks

checks.claim: 4. For host-to-disk demotion, the item at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has the highest priority to be evicted (the scan runs tail to head).
checks.correction: The tail-to-head scan and tail-first preference are stated. 'Highest' overstates it in two ways. (1) The general rule uses the comparative 'higher priority'. (2) In the Fig. 9 walkthrough, the scan runs only after a first check of whether every host-memory KV has an associated job in the queue. That implies a host-resident KV with no queued job would be considered before the tail scan, though the paper never spells out that branch. So tail-of-window comes first only among host-resident KVs whose jobs are in the window. The paper also says nothing about host-resident KVs whose jobs are queued beyond the window. In Fig. 9 the victim is Job 4, third of six in the window. It is chosen because it is the host-resident KV nearest the tail: KV 7 is already on disk, and no KV 5 or KV 6 appears in DRAM.
checks.quote: "When CachedAttention evicts one item from the host memory to disks, the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted." ... "First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue. It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail. Therefore, the KV cache for Job 4 is selected to be evicted from the host memory to the disks."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: 5. In the paper's Fig. 9 example, when the disk is full, the KV of the last-arrived queued job outside the size-6 window (Job 9) is dropped out of the system.
checks.correction: Confirmed by the text and the figure together. Fig. 9 draws the 'eviction window, size: 6' brace over Job 2 to Job 7, so Jobs 8 and 9 lie outside it. 'Outside the window' comes from the figure, not the prose. KV 9 sits on disk with an arrow leaving the disks box, and KV 4 takes its place. The prose says 'most suitable candidate to be evicted'. 'Out of the system' follows from the general rule that a full disk evicts KVs 'out of the system'. Job 9 is still in the queue, so the KV of a queued job outside the window is dropped. Among the two jobs outside the window (8 and 9), the last-arrived one is chosen.
checks.quote: "Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted. Finally, the KV cache for Job 4 is moved to the location previously occupied by Job 9." (and earlier: "if the disks are full, we also need to evict some KV caches stored in the disks out of the system.")
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: 6. The paper does not specify the eviction order among cached sessions that have no queued job.
checks.correction: Correct. No ordering rule (LRU, FIFO, size or anything else) is given for sessions without a queued job. LRU and FIFO appear only as baselines. Two nearby facts are worth knowing. (a) The Fig. 9 walkthrough first checks whether host-memory KVs all have a queued job, which implies such sessions are demoted ahead of queued ones, with no tie-break among them. (b) §4.3.6 gives each session's KV a TTL, a maximum saving time since last access, set to one hour in that experiment. TTL is time-based expiry, not an eviction order under capacity pressure.
checks.quote: "First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue." (§3.3.2) ... "In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access. The TTL is set as the unit time mentioned above." ... "In the experiment, we set the TTL to one hour." (§4.3.6)
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; §4.3.6 The Cache Capacity Requirement

checks.claim: CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer so pre-loading can start while the previous job is still running, and sizes it as Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew); imperfect overlap occurs when Tload·Lhist > Tpref·Lnew.
checks.correction: Matches the paper. One nuance: the paper introduces the buffer in two steps. First, a read buffer closes the gap between jobs. Second, a 'customized larger pre-loading buffer' covers imperfect overlap, and the Sbuf formula sizes this larger buffer (B = PCIe bandwidth; Tload and Tpref are per-token load and prefill times). The evaluation treats both as one read buffer of varying size (PL-B0 to PL-B15). Wording is identical in arXiv v3 (30 Jun 2024), USENIX ATC'24 and v1.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap. Specifically, as shown in Figure 6c, with the read buffer, the read stream doesn't have to wait for the release of the execution buffer from the last job. The read stream can start the pre-loading while the last job is running." ... "The overhead can be further minimized by employing a customized larger pre-loading buffer." ... "Imperfect overlapping happens when Tload Lhist > Tpref Lnew, which indicates that the transmission time is larger than the partial prefilling time. The buffer is used to fill up the time gap Tload Lhist − Tpref Lnew. Combined with the PCIe bandwidth B, the buffer size can be set by the following formula: Sbuf = B(Tload Lhist − Tpref Lnew)."
checks.section: §3.2.1 Layer-wise Pre-loading from Memory to HBMs (Figures 6c, 7b)

checks.claim: In CachedAttention's micro-benchmark (LLaMA-13B, 1K history + 100 new tokens), layer-wise pre-loading without a read buffer (PL-B0) reduced prefill time by 35%, and with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15) by 61%.
checks.correction: Correct. Both reductions are measured against NO-PL (no pre-loading, which counts KV load time plus compute time). The setup is LLaMA-13B on a single GPU with batch size 16. The text writes 'PF-B15' (a typo), while the Figure 19 axis label is PL-B15. The paper says PL-B15 'perfectly overlaps' the load time.
checks.quote: "The model used is LLaMA-13B with a single GPU and the batch size is set to 16. Layer-wise KV cache pre-loading. We set the length of historical tokens to 1K and the length of newly input tokens to 100 ... e.g., PL-B0 indicates no read buffer and PF-B5 indicates a read buffer size of 5 layers of KV cache. We observe although there is no read buffer, i.e., PL-B0, the pre-loading scheme reduces the prefilling time by 35% compared to NO-PL. PF-B15 perfectly overlaps the KV cache loading time and reduces the prefilling time by 61% compared to NO-PL."
checks.section: §4.3.2 Overlapped KV cache Access (Figure 19)

checks.claim: CachedAttention saves KV from HBM to host memory asynchronously: prefill KV is written layer by layer and overlapped with decoding, decode KV is written layer by layer while decoding, and unfinished writes go to a reserved HBM write buffer so the next job is not blocked.
checks.correction: Correct. Minor wording point: for prefill, the paper says the write stream 'retains' the KV cache layer by layer and that this KV 'can be overlapped with the decoding phase'. It does not literally say 'written'. Figure 8b shows the prefill KV being written during decode.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention needs to save KV caches to host memory to enable the reuse of the KV caches across conversations." ... "for the prefilling phase, as each self-attention operation can produce a significant amount of KV cache, the write stream retains the KV cache layer by layer. The KV cache produced by the prefilling phase can be overlapped with the decoding phase. For the decoding phase, as the KV cache is iteratively produced, the write stream writes back the KV cache layer by layer while decoding. To avoid getting stuck if the KV cached is not fully written back when the decoding is already finished, we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching. The unfinished KV caches are temporarily moved to the write buffer to avoid blocking the execution of the next job."
checks.section: §3.2.2 Asynchronous Saving from HBMs to Memory (Figure 8)

checks.claim: CachedAttention rejects writing all KV after the turn ends because the saving time would be on the critical path, and reports that asynchronous saving cut total execution time by 13-15%.
checks.correction: Correct. 'Rejects' is a fair paraphrase: the paper calls end-of-turn writing the 'baseline method' and says it 'potentially delays' the next jobs. The 13-15% cut is in 'overall execution time'. It comes from a micro-benchmark: LLaMA-13B, single GPU, batch 16, prompt lengths 1K to 1.6K, 20 decoding steps. It is not an end-to-end result.
checks.quote: "A baseline method to save the KV caches is to write all produced KV caches together after the round of conversation ends. This method however potentially delays the execution of the next scheduled jobs since the KV saving time is on the critical path of inference, as shown in Figure 8a." ... "We set different prompt lengths ranging from 1K to 1.6K and the number of decoding steps to 20 ... CachedAttention employs the asynchronous saving scheme allowing KV cache saving to overlap with inference execution, reducing the overall execution time by 13% to 15%."
checks.section: §3.2.2 (Figure 8a) and §4.3.2 Asynchronous KV cache saving (Figure 20)

checks.claim: In CachedAttention, HBM holds the execution buffer plus read and write buffers and is not used as a cross-turn cache tier; keeping KV in HBM only is evaluated as a baseline.
checks.correction: Supported, with caveats. (a) The paper names the HBM execution, read and write buffers, but it never lists everything HBM holds. The exclusion of HBM is drawn from how it defines AttentionStore (host memory and disks) and from §4.3.7, which contrasts 'caching KVs on HBMs' with 'CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs'. There is no explicit rule such as 'HBM is not a tier'. (b) One intro sentence leaves a small opening: previous jobs' KV is moved out of HBM 'if the HBM space is not enough'. The paper never describes reusing HBM-resident KV across turns. (c) There are two baselines, not one: HBM-only (a 10GB HBM cache) and HBM+DRAM. Their hit rates are about 0% and 1.7-19.1%; CA reaches 71-90%.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention employs multi-tier cost-effective storage mediums in AttentionStore, i.e., host memory and disks." (§3.1) ... "Some existing works [18,28,63] employ only the HBM space for caching the KV caches of multi-turn conversations. We here compare the performance of mechanism caching KVs on HBMs with that of CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs. In the experiments, we configure the size of the HBM cache as 10GB, the size of DRAM as 128GB, and the size of SSDs as 10TB ... The hit rate of the HBM-only caching method is nearly 0% for all models due to the limited capacity of HBM. Using HBM with DRAM improves the cache hit rate to 3.4%, 1.7%, 7.7%, and 19.1%" (§4.3.7). Caveat from §1: "the subsequent inference jobs need to wait until the KV caches from the previous jobs are moved out of the HBMs if the HBM space is not enough."
checks.section: §3.1 Overview (Figure 5), §3.2.1/§3.2.2 (HBM execution/read/write buffers), §4.3.7 Impact of Caching Storage Mediums (Figure 24), §1
